short_description: Baldwin County prohibits wind energy systems with a capacity of 50 kW or greater and requires setbacks from scenic byways.
long_description: Baldwin County, Alabama has enacted zoning ordinances that prohibit wind energy systems with a capacity of 50 kW or greater. Additionally, any wind energy system located near a scenic byway or corridor must not cause an adverse visual impact.

short_description: Cherokee County enacted restrictions on wind power including noise limits and setbacks.
long_description: In 2014, the Alabama state legislature enacted S.B. 402 which established certain restrictions on wind power in Cherokee County, including a noise limit of 40 decibels (dBA) at the nearest property line and a setback of at least 2,500 feet from the nearest property line.

adopted_or_event_date_text: Not explicitly stated but likely around 2014-2019
short_description: DeKalb County requires wind turbines to be set back 2,500 feet from property lines and noise must not exceed 40 decibels.
long_description: In DeKalb County, Alabama, wind turbines must be set back 2,500 feet from property lines and noise must not exceed 40 decibels. Additionally, any wind energy system or turbine that does not operate continuously for 365 consecutive days may be deemed abandoned and shall be removed by the operator of the system.

short_description: Etowah County enacted restrictions on wind power including noise limits and setbacks.
long_description: In 2014, the Alabama state legislature enacted S.B. 403 which established certain restrictions on wind power in Etowah County, including a noise limit of 40 decibels (dBA) at the nearest property line and a setback of at least 2,500 feet from the nearest property line.

short_description: Pioneer Green Energy abandoned plans for a wind project in Etowah County after local residents filed a lawsuit and state restrictions were enacted.
long_description: In August 2014, Pioneer Green Energy, a Texas-based developer, abandoned plans to construct a $160 million wind project comprising 35 to 40 turbines after local residents filed a lawsuit challenging the project and after the state enacted onerous restrictions on wind energy in Etowah County.

short_description: Local residents opposed a proposed solar farm in Covington County citing concerns about the impact on family properties and well water supplies.
long_description: Local residents expressed strong opposition to a proposed 160-MW, 1,000-acre solar panel array at an August 21, 2023 meeting. The residents opposed the farm for several reasons, including that it would be powering communities over an hour away and not their own; that the solar farm might encroach on family properties that have existed for generations; and that potential road runoff might impact their well water supplies.

short_description: Pioneer Green Energy abandoned plans for a wind project in Cherokee County after local residents filed a lawsuit and state restrictions were enacted.
long_description: In August 2014, Pioneer Green Energy abandoned plans to construct a $40 million wind project comprising 7 to 8 turbines in Cherokee County after local residents filed a lawsuit challenging the project and after the state enacted onerous restrictions on wind energy in Cherokee County.

short_description: Native Energy Solutions abandoned plans for a wind project in Cleburne County after local residents filed a lawsuit.
long_description: In October 2015, Native Energy Solutions, an Oklahoma-based developer, announced that it was no longer planning to build a wind project in Cleburne County. The project faced opposition from local residents who, in June 2014, filed a lawsuit seeking a permanent injunction that would bar the developer from constructing wind turbines in the county.

short_description: Coolidge City approved a zoning amendment to remove solar farms from agricultural districts and created an industrial solar farm overlay zone.
long_description: In May 2022, the Coolidge City Council in Pinal County, Arizona, approved a zoning amendment removing solar farms from approved uses in agricultural districts. At the same time, the council voted to create an industrial solar farm overlay zone to identify areas in the city for developing solar farms. In October 2023, Mohave County established a 240-day moratorium on using energy overlay re-zoning for renewable energy development.

short_description: Mohave County Board of Supervisors established a 240-day moratorium on energy overlay re-zoning for renewable projects, which was later lifted.
long_description: In October 2023, the Mohave County Board of Supervisors in Arizona cast a 3-2 vote to establish a 240-day moratorium on using energy overlay re-zoning for the development of renewable energy on private property. Prior to this, the Board had denied every application for energy overlay re-zoning. In June 2024, the Board voted 3-2 in favor of allowing solar projects within the county on land zoned for ‘Light Industrial’ use, effectively lifting the moratorium.

short_description: Nature and People First sought to develop a utility-scale pumped storage hydropower project, facing opposition from local residents and environmental groups.
long_description: The developer Nature and People First has sought to develop a 6,000-MW, utility-scale pumped storage hydropower project on approximately 400 acres of land in Apache and Navajo Counties. In July 2023, three organizations submitted a letter to FERC attaching resolutions against the project from 18 Navajo Nation chapters and agencies. Nearby residents had expressed concerns about potential damage to underground water supplies and sacred lands, and that the developer had not sufficiently involved nearby residents. In February 2024, FERC denied applications for a preliminary permit for the project.

short_description: A special use permit for a solar farm was denied by the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission.
long_description: On September 11, 2024, the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission voted to deny a special use permit to construct a 75-MW solar farm on 597 acres of land. The commission chairwoman stated that they had too many solar projects in the county now.

short_description: The SunZia transmission line faced legal challenges from tribes and environmental groups over its routing in the San Pedro Valley.
long_description: The SunZia transmission line, expected to open in 2026 with the ability to carry more than 3,600 MW of wind power generated in New Mexico wind farms, routed through the San Pedro Valley. The Tohono O’odham, Hopi, Zuni, and San Carlos Apache tribes claimed that the Bureau of Land Management ignored over 15 years of attempts by the tribes to recognize the valley as a culturally significant area. In January 2024, these tribes, along with Center for Biological Diversity and Archeology Southwest, filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona, claiming that the review of the project violated NEPA and the NHPA. The lawsuit was dismissed in June 2024 and subsequently appealed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.

short_description: Madison County Quorum Court passed a one-year moratorium on wind development within the county in December 2024.
long_description: In December 2024, the Madison County Quorum Court unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on wind development within the county.

short_description: Stop Wind Farms group opposed the 180-MW Nimbus Wind Farm in Carroll County, Arkansas.
long_description: In 2016, Scout Clean Energy began negotiating contracts with landowners for the 180-MW Nimbus Wind Farm, which would cover 14 square miles of land atop the Ozark Mountains. In 2023, a group called Stop Wind Farms was formed to oppose this development and collected over 1,000 verified signatures in opposition, raising concerns about disturbances to the aesthetic value of the Ozark ridgeline and decreased property values. Nevertheless, on September 17, 2024, the Carroll County Quorum Court approved Scout to use county roads for installation, so long as Scout covered the cost for road maintenance around the wind farm.

short_description: Protect Our Pocketbooks opposed the Wind Catcher Energy Connection Project in Washington County, Arkansas.
long_description: In July 2018, American Electric Power abandoned plans to build a $4.5 billion, 2,000-MW wind farm in the Oklahoma panhandle, as well as an associated interstate transmission project that would have delivered electricity to Arkansas and other states. In Arkansas, a dark money group called Protect Our Pocketbooks paid for television advertisements claiming that Arkansas would receive no benefits from the project. The developer responded by issuing a statement that Protect Our Pocketbooks was “presenting misleading information to the public, including manipulation of statements by Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson.” Although the Arkansas Public Service Commission ultimately granted approval for the Arkansas components of the project, the Wind Catcher project was canceled altogether when the Texas Public Service Commission denied approval.

short_description: Multiple bans and prohibitions on wind, solar, and storage projects were enacted in California between 2018-2020.
long_description: Between 2018 and 2020, various local jurisdictions within California implemented bans or prohibitions on the development of renewable energy projects such as wind, solar, and storage facilities. These measures were often driven by concerns over land use, aesthetics, and environmental impacts.

short_description: City of Escondido implemented a 45-day moratorium on battery energy storage sites to update regulations.
long_description: On October 9, 2024, the City of Escondido put in place a 45-day moratorium on battery energy storage sites in order to update regulations to account for safety risks.

short_description: Crescent City prohibits small wind energy conversion systems in certain areas.
long_description: Small wind energy conversion systems are not permitted on vacant lots; on a site listed in the National Register of Historic Places or the California Register of Historic Resources; where the system would be visible from any coastal scenic resource area; within 100 feet of any sensitive or endangered habitat designated by the California Department of Fish and Game without written permission from that agency; or within any public right-of-way, easement, path of travel, or interior traffic circulation system.

short_description: Los Angeles County prohibits utility-scale wind and solar projects in certain areas.
long_description: The Los Angeles County Code prohibits “[u]tility-scale wind energy facilities.” The code also prohibits ground-mounted utility-scale solar energy facilities in designated areas of ecological and economic importance.

short_description: San Bernardino County banned utility-oriented renewable energy projects in rural living areas.
long_description: In 2019, the San Bernardino County Board of Supervisors banned “utility oriented” renewable energy projects in designated “rural living” areas covering more than 1,000,000 acres of land. Residential solar panels and community solar projects are not affected.

short_description: Santa Clara County prohibits solar farms in certain agricultural areas.
long_description: In 2010, Santa Clara County adopted an ordinance that prohibits solar farms from land designated as “Agriculture—Large scale”; the ordinance also prohibits solar farms from land designated as “Agriculture—Medium scale,” unless the land is deemed to be of “marginal quality for agricultural purposes.”

project_or_policy_name: Altamont Pass Wind Resource Area First-Generation Wind Farms
short_description: A lawsuit was brought against the operators of wind turbines in Altamont Pass, alleging bird deaths.
long_description: In 2004, the Center for Biological Diversity brought a lawsuit against the operators of wind turbines in the Altamont Pass Wind Resource Area in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, alleging that the “obsolete, first-generation wind turbine generators” being used at the site were killing and injuring birds in violation of the public trust doctrine. The lawsuit was dismissed, and the dismissal was upheld on appeal.

short_description: Local groups opposed two solar projects, leading to legal challenges and appeals.
long_description: Opponents of two North Livermore Valley solar projects, Aramis (410 acres) and Sunwalker (70 acres), led by a group called Save North Livermore Valley, argued that the proposed locations of the projects impinge on agriculture, natural wildlife habitat, open space, and visual and scenic resources. In October 2020, two candidates running for election to the Alameda County Board of Supervisors issued a joint statement urging the board to place a moratorium on solar development on agricultural land. After the East County Board of Zoning Adjustments approved both projects, local groups stated appealed both decisions. By December 2020, three local organizations had filed appeals challenging the approval of the Aramis project. In May 2022, the Alameda County Superior Court upheld the county’s approval of the Aramis project, dismissing a lawsuit by project opponents. In July 2023, Save North Livermore Valley appealed the Superior Court’s decision. California’s First District Court of Appeals denied the appeal in August 2023.

short_description: Local community members opposed the Aratina Solar Center project due to wildlife and Joshua Tree concerns.
long_description: In October 2021, the Kern County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved the Aratina Solar Center, a solar-plus-storage project including 530 MW of solar capacity and 600 MW of battery energy storage capacity. Shortly thereafter, local community members organized a petition that received 51,000 signatures. A primary concern driving local opposition to the project is the potential impact on local wildlife and on Joshua Trees. In compliance with the California Western Joshua Tree Conservation Act, the developer received an Incidental Take Permit, which authorized the developer to remove trees with an option to pay a standard mitigation fee rather than complete mitigation fee.

short_description: The Blythe Mesa Solar Power Project faced legal challenges over government-to-government consultation.
long_description: The Blythe Mesa Solar Power Project is a 465-MW solar farm built between 2010 and 2020 over 4,070 acres of BLM land by the developer NextEra. The Colorado River Indian Tribe (CRIT) sued the Department of Interior in 2014 in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, claiming that BLM’s lack of government-to-government consultation violated the NHPA; the lawsuit also included claims under NEPA and the Federal Land Policy and Management Act. The District Court granted summary judgment in favor of the Department of Interior in July 2015.

short_description: Residents challenged the Boulder Brush Project, alleging violations of environmental laws.
long_description: The Boulder Brush Project is a 320-acre substation and transmission line proposed by Terra-Gen, which would connect to the 60-turbine Campo Wind Project planned for the Campo Indian Reservation. In March 2021, the San Diego County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved the project. Residents consequently formed an organization called Backcountry Against Dumps to challenge the decision. In April 2021, the organization filed a lawsuit claiming that the project violated the California Environmental Quality Act and various planning and zoning regulations. The lawsuit contended that the County’s environmental review of the project did not fully analyze the risks to wildlife and groundwater and the effects of noise disruptions. In March 2024, the Fourth District Court of Appeal vacated the San Diego Superior Court’s dismissal of the lawsuit, instructing the trial court to allow the case to proceed.

short_description: Local conservation groups and the Northern Chumash Tribe opposed the proposed offshore wind project.
long_description: In 2022, local conservation groups and members of the Northern Chumash Tribe mobilized to oppose the proposed 40-MW BW-IDEOL Vandenberg Space Force Base Pilot offshore wind project off the coast of Santa Barbara County, which would have consisted of four floating turbines. The project site is in an area the Northern Chumash Tribe have sought to designate as

short_description: State-level prohibitions on wind and solar projects have been adopted in Colorado.
long_description: Colorado has implemented state-level prohibitions on the construction of new wind and solar energy facilities, which have faced opposition from various stakeholders. These restrictions were adopted between 2019 and 2023 and are currently in force. Legal challenges to these prohibitions have been filed by affected parties.

project_or_policy_name: Moratorium on applications for commercial-scale renewable energy facilities
short_description: Delta County imposed a 6-month moratorium on applications for commercial-scale renewable energy facilities, extended as of December 2023.
long_description: In September 2022, Delta County Board of County Commissioners imposed a 6-month moratorium on applications for commercial-scale renewable energy facilities. The moratorium was later extended and remained in effect as of December 2023.

short_description: Mesa County approved a six-month moratorium on commercial solar projects, which ended after new regulations were adopted in April 2024.
long_description: In January 2024, Mesa County Board of Commissioners approved a six-month moratorium on commercial solar projects to provide time to update local zoning regulations. The moratorium was lifted when the board approved new regulations in April 2024.

project_or_policy_name: Moratorium on processing applications for power generation facilities
short_description: Montrose County imposed a 6-month moratorium on processing applications for power generation facilities, extended in April and December 2023.
long_description: In October 2022, Montrose County Board of County Commissioners imposed a 6-month moratorium on the processing of applications for power generation facilities. The moratorium did not apply to solar panels or other renewable energy components installed on private residential or commercial structures. In April 2023, the moratorium was extended for 18 months and again in December 2024 by another 6 months.

project_or_policy_name: Moratorium on wind and solar projects
short_description: Rio Blanco County adopted a moratorium on wind and solar projects to determine how to incorporate such projects into the county’s land use plan.
long_description: In August 2023, Rio Blanco Board of County Commissioners adopted a moratorium on wind and solar projects in order to determine how to incorporate such projects into the county's land use plan.

project_or_policy_name: Moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects (including solar)
short_description: San Miguel County enacted a 6-month moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects, including solar, which was extended and ended after new zoning regulations were adopted in September 2024.
long_description: In May 2023, San Miguel County Board of Commissioners enacted a 6-month moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects (including solar), scheduled to expire in November 2024 after being extended twice. In September 2024, the Board unanimously adopted new zoning regulations on solar projects, ending the moratorium.

project_or_policy_name: Moratorium on accepting, processing, and approving wind and solar farm permits
short_description: Washington County imposed a temporary moratorium on accepting, processing, and approving wind and solar farm permits in unincorporated parts of the county.
long_description: A temporary moratorium on accepting, processing, and approving wind and solar farm permits in unincorporated parts of Washington County went into effect on March 24, 2020. The moratorium was extended multiple times until August 31, 2021 or later.

short_description: Connecticut has state-level opposition to wind and solar projects, with a ban in place.
long_description: From 2019 to 2023, Connecticut faced significant opposition to renewable energy projects, particularly wind and solar installations. A state-wide ban on new utility-scale wind projects was implemented during this period, leading to legal challenges from various stakeholders.

short_description: Prohibits solar photovoltaic projects of 2 MW or greater on core forest or prime farmland unless state regulators find no material effect.
long_description: In 2017, the Connecticut Legislature enacted Public Act No. 17-218, which prohibits solar photovoltaic projects of 2 MW or greater on 'core forest' or 'prime farmland' statewide unless state regulators find that the project will not ‘materially affect’ the land’s status as core forest or prime farmland.

short_description: Developer appealed Connecticut Siting Council’s rejection of 1.5-MW solar project citing tree removal concerns.
long_description: In August 2024, the Connecticut Siting Council unanimously rejected a plan for a 1.5-MW solar project on Denslow Hill Road in New Haven County, citing concerns over the developer’s plans to remove about 7.9 acres of trees. In September 2024, the developer filed an appeal to the decision.

short_description: Residents challenged Connecticut Siting Council’s approval of 4-MW solar facility citing aviation safety concerns.
long_description: In August 2024, the Connecticut Siting Council denied a petition to build a 4-MW solar facility in Ellington Airport due to uncertainty about its effects on air navigation and aviation safety. Residents cited concerns about potential impacts of a solar facility on a local parachuting landing site near the proposed solar site.

project_or_policy_name: Fairfield to Congress Railroad Transmission Line
short_description: City of Bridgeport appealed Connecticut Siting Council’s approval of transmission line project citing evidence against it.
long_description: The Fairfield to Congress Railroad Transmission Line project proposes to replace transmission lines along the railroad corridor, with the goal of improving reliability and resilience in the regional electric grid. After the Connecticut Siting Council approved the project, the City of Bridgeport filed an appeal of the decision, citing ‘reliable, prohibitive, and substantial evidence introduced opposing the project.’

project_or_policy_name: TRITEC America’s Carter Street Solar Project
short_description: Connecticut Siting Council rejected 0.999-MW solar facility citing environmental and residential concerns.
long_description: In October 2024, the Connecticut Siting Council unanimously rejected an application for a 0.999-MW solar facility in Manchester on Carter Street. The project would have been sited on 7.8 acres of forested land in an area zoned for rural residential development. Local opponents raised concerns about the environmental impact of cutting down trees and the project’s proximity to houses.

short_description: Kent County imposed a moratorium and later prohibited new solar farms larger than 50 acres on agricultural land.
long_description: In March 2022, the Kent County Levy Court imposed a moratorium on new solar projects in response to opposition. In September 2022, the court amended the ordinance to prohibit new solar farms larger than 50 acres on agricultural land, reducing available land from 75,000 acres to 1,500 acres. A moratorium was also voted for utility-scale wind farms in anticipation of a future decision.

short_description: Bethany Beach town ordinance prohibits commercial solar installations on agricultural land.
long_description: A town ordinance in Bethany Beach, Sussex County, Delaware, prohibits commercial solar installations whose main purpose is to generate energy for sale back into the energy system. This restriction was enacted after opposition from residents and groups.

short_description: A lawsuit was filed to challenge the approval of a 100-MW solar project on agricultural land.
long_description: In March 2022, a landowner and a group called Citizens Against Solar Pollution filed a lawsuit in Delaware Chancery Court challenging Kent County’s approval of the proposed 100-MW Cedar Creek Solar project. The lawsuit alleged environmental damage, reduced property values, disruption to rural character, and threats to historical artifacts.

short_description: Frankford Town Council denied a solar farm application due to non-compliance with the town’s 2020 Comprehensive Plan.
long_description: In May 2024, the Frankford Town Council voted to deny an application for a 44-acre solar farm proposed by Dukes Farm Limited Partnership. The decision came after a public meeting where local residents expressed reservations about the project. The denial was based on the application not meeting certain criteria in the town’s 2020 Comprehensive Plan, such as maintaining a small-town feel.

project_or_policy_name: Skipjack Wind Farm Interconnection Facility in Fenwick State Park
short_description: The Skipjack Wind Farm abandoned plans to connect to the grid at Fenwick Island State Park due to opposition.
long_description: The proposed offshore wind project, Skipjack Wind Farm, was originally planned to connect to the grid at a facility in Delaware’s Fenwick Island State Park. The plan received pushback from the Delaware Chapter of the Surfrider Foundation, who argued that installing transmission infrastructure in a state park was contrary to the mission of the Delaware Division of Parks and Recreation. In 2020, the developer abandoned plans to site the interconnection facility at Fenwick Island State Park.

short_description: A lawsuit was filed to halt the operation of a wind turbine used for research by the University of Delaware.
long_description: A Lewes resident filed two lawsuits in state and federal court to halt the operation of a wind turbine used for research by the University of Delaware, arguing that backroom dealings led to an expedited approval process. The federal lawsuit was dismissed in January 2015. In the state lawsuit, the Delaware Court of Chancery granted summary judgment against the plaintiff on multiple claims in December 2015, which the Delaware Supreme Court affirmed in August 2016.

project_or_policy_name: US Wind Substation Project in Dagsboro
short_description: Sussex County Council denied a conditional use permit for an offshore wind substation project.
long_description: The Sussex County Council denied a conditional use permit that would allow US Wind to build a substation in Dagsboro to support its offshore wind project. The offshore wind project consists of 121 wind turbines and up to four offshore substations. The council cited lack of direct benefits to the residents of Sussex County among the reasons for denial.

short_description: Florida enacted a state law prohibiting the construction or expansion of wind energy facilities in specific areas.
long_description: In 2024, Florida enacted a state statute that prohibits the construction or expansion of any wind energy facility offshore; within 1 mile of the coastline; within 1 mile of intercoastal waterways; on any waters or submerged lands. This law is effective and in force.

short_description: Alachua County commissioners denied a permit for a proposed solar project citing community outreach and property value concerns.
long_description: In October 2020, Alachua County commissioners voted to deny a permit for the Archer Solar Project, a 75-MW, 643-acre solar facility by First Solar and Duke Energy. The denial was based on a lack of outreach to the historically Black community where the project was to be located and concerns about impacts on property values.

short_description: Alachua County commissioners denied a permit for the Sand Bluff Solar Project citing community outreach concerns.
long_description: In July 2021, Alachua County commissioners voted to disallow the proposed Sand Bluff Solar Project on 600 acres outside of Archer, Florida. Opposition against the project centered on lack of outreach to the historically Black community in which it was to be sited. The local chapters of the NAACP and Sierra Club opposed the project, while the Climate Reality Project and the local chapter of the League of Women Voters supported it.

short_description: The Archer Solar Project faced opposition from the historically Black community and was denied a permit in October 2020.
long_description: In October 2020, Alachua County commissioners voted to deny a permit for the proposed 75-MW, 643-acre solar project by First Solar and Duke Energy. The denial was based on concerns about community outreach and impacts on property values in the historically Black community where the project was to be located.

short_description: The Sand Bluff Solar Project faced opposition from the NAACP and Sierra Club, but was ultimately denied a permit in July 2021.
long_description: In July 2021, Alachua County commissioners voted to disallow the proposed Sand Bluff Solar Project on 600 acres outside of Archer, Florida. Opposition against the project centered on lack of outreach to the historically Black community in which it was to be sited. The local chapters of the NAACP and Sierra Club opposed the project, while the Climate Reality Project and the local chapter of the League of Women Voters supported it.

short_description: Baldwin County adopted an ordinance requiring solar farms to be set back at least 300 feet from dwelling units and property lines.
long_description: An ordinance was adopted on June 16, 2020, in Baldwin County, Georgia, which requires that solar farms be set back at least 300 feet from dwelling units and at least 300 feet from property lines under most circumstances. Adjacent parcel owners can agree to a smaller setback.

short_description: Franklin County adopted an indefinite ban on commercial energy facilities.
long_description: In April 2022, the Franklin County Commission in Georgia adopted an indefinite ban on commercial energy facilities within the county.

short_description: Grady County imposed a 60-day moratorium on solar farm applications.
long_description: In February 2017, Grady County in Georgia imposed a 60-day moratorium on solar farm applications. The moratorium was later lifted and replaced by an ordinance providing setback requirements for solar farms.

project_or_policy_name: Ordinance on solar farm visibility and setbacks
short_description: Greene County adopted an ordinance restricting solar farm visibility and requiring setbacks from homes, churches, and public facilities.
long_description: An ordinance was last updated on December 8, 2020, in Greene County, Georgia. The ordinance restricts the visibility of solar farms from any portion of the right-of-way of adjacent public roads or common boundary lines of adjacent property. It also requires that solar farms be set back at least 500 feet from existing homes, churches, and public facilities, and at least 350 feet from property lines.

project_or_policy_name: Ban on new solar farms except for personal use
short_description: Jeff Davis County banned new solar farms except for personal use.
long_description: In June 2023, the Jeff Davis County Commission in Georgia amended its Land Use Ordinance to ban new solar farms, with an exception for those used for personal use.

short_description: Lee County placed a moratorium on solar farm construction in response to increased interest from developers.
long_description: In May 2019, Lee County officials in Georgia placed a moratorium on solar farm construction. The moratorium was extended through January 2021 and then lifted when the county adopted an amendment to its Zoning Ordinance of Solar Energy Systems.

project_or_policy_name: 6-month moratorium on new solar projects, followed by ordinance amendment
short_description: Oglethorpe County adopted a 6-month moratorium on new solar projects, followed by an amendment to its Zoning Ordinance.
long_description: In March 2023, the Oglethorpe County Board of Commissioners in Georgia adopted a 6-month moratorium on new solar projects. The moratorium lasted until September 2023 when the county adopted an amendment to its Zoning Ordinance of Solar Energy Systems.

project_or_policy_name: Indefinite moratorium on solar energy facility construction
short_description: Thomas County implemented an indefinite moratorium on solar energy facility construction.
long_description: In October 2016, Thomas County in Georgia placed a moratorium on solar installaDons. The moratorium was extended through May 2017 and then voted unanimously to implement an indefinite moratorium on solar energy facility construcDon in October 2018.

short_description: The Macon-Bibb Planning and Zoning Commission rejected Cubico Sustainable Investments' plan for a 780-MW solar farm.
long_description: On May 23, 2022, the Macon-Bibb Planning and Zoning Commission in Georgia unanimously rejected Cubico Sustainable Investments’ plan for a 780-MW solar farm. The rejection was based on concerns about harm to wildlife, damage to roads, and potential declining property values. Opponents collected 400 signatures against the project.

short_description: The Sumter County Planning & Zoning Board recommended denying a conditional use permit for SA Solar’s proposed solar farm.
long_description: In November 2023, the Sumter County Planning & Zoning Board in Georgia recommended that the county Board of Commissioners deny a conditional use permit for SA Solar’s proposed solar farm. The recommendation was set aside by the Board of Commissioners in December 2023 and a conditional use permit was granted.

short_description: Houston County Commissioners denied a permit for Silicon Ranch to construct a solar farm near the Oaky Woods Wildlife Management Area.
long_description: On September 3, 2024, the Houston County Commissioners in Georgia voted to deny a permit to developer Silicon Ranch to construct a 4,700-acre solar farm in Kathleen. The proposal faced opposition from local naturalists due to its proximity to the Oaky Woods Wildlife Management Area, which hosts a regionally significant population of black bears.

short_description: The Houston County Board of Commissioners denied an application for a 4,700-acre solar farm due to concerns about quality of living and wildlife habitat.
long_description: The Houston County Board of Commissioners in Georgia unanimously denied an application for a 4,700-acre project. Among the reasons for denial were concerns about the quality of living, property values, and wildlife habitat, particularly bear habitat. At the Board of Zoning Appeals meeting, there was strong opposition from residents.

short_description: The Honolulu City Council revised land use regulations for wind power, increasing setbacks and prohibiting height changes after contract end.
long_description: In December 2024, the Honolulu City Council of Hawaii revised its land use regulations to increase the required setback distance from certain property lines for wind turbines. The new regulation mandates a setback of 1.25 miles or ten times the turbine’s height—whichever is greater. Additionally, the council decided against allowing wind turbines to make repairs affecting their height after the end of their contracts.

project_or_policy_name: Kahuku Na Pua Makani Wind Project
short_description: Local opposition led to a reduction in the scope of the wind project and legal challenges over species protection.
long_description: The Kahuku Na Pua Makani Wind Project, initially planned for 13-15 turbines, was reduced to 8 turbines due to local opposition. Legal challenges included a contested case hearing petition by Keep the North Shore Country in 2016 and an appeal of the Board of Land and Natural Resources' decision in 2019. The state Circuit Court upheld the decision in May 2019, and the Supreme Court of Hawaii affirmed it in February 2022.

short_description: Legal challenges and a settlement led to enhanced research plans for the wind farm project.
long_description: The Kawailoa Wind Farm sought to amend its Habitat Conservation Plan (HCP) and Incidental Take License (ITL) in 2018. In 2019, the state Board of Land and Natural Resources approved the amendments. Environmental group Keep the North Shore Country challenged the amendments as inadequate for wildlife protection. A settlement was reached in January 2021, with Kawailoa agreeing to fund an enhanced research plan.

short_description: Environmental and resident opposition led to the cancellation of a solar farm project.
long_description: In November 2023, Innergex Energy cancelled development of a 15-MW solar farm planned for Maui Meadows in South Maui. The project faced opposition from environmentalists and residents due to concerns about water pollution, flooding, wildfire risks, and loss of open, scenic land.

short_description: Bannock County enacted a moratorium and ordinance banning large-scale solar farms and limiting wind turbines.
long_description: In October 2023, Bannock County Board of Commissioners enacted a 180-day moratorium on permits for large-scale energy projects. In March 2024, the board enacted an ordinance that bans solar farms capable of producing 10 MW or more, storing 10 MW or more, or encompassing 100 acres or more. The ordinance also categorically bans commercial-scale wind turbines and limits non-commercial wind turbines to two per lot.

short_description: Bingham County requires commercial wind turbines to be set back from property lines and town sites.
long_description: Under a 2012 ordinance, commercial wind turbines must be set back at least three times the tower height from the exterior line of the project unless an agreement with affected property owners is reached. In all instances, the setback must be at least 1.5 times the tower height. Further, commercial wind turbines must be set back an additional one mile from 'all placed town sites and/or incorporated cities.'

short_description: Bonneville County significantly restricted wind development to a specific turbine zone in the southern part of the county.
long_description: In 2010, Bonneville County Planning and Zoning Commission significantly restricted wind development to a specific 'turbine zone' in the southern portion of the county. However, the current version of the ordinance does not appear to reference this restricted zone.

short_description: Twin Falls County instituted a moratorium on large-scale energy projects and passed zoning regulations to regulate wind and solar projects.
long_description: In August 2023, Twin Falls County Commissioners voted to institute a moratorium on large-scale energy projects on private land for 182 days. The county defined 'large scale' as those with a nameplate capacity of 10 MW or greater or requiring 100 acres or more of land. In March 2024, the Twin Falls County Commissioners unanimously passed a zoning ordinance regulating wind and solar energy projects. The ordinance prohibits new energy projects from being located on prime farmland, which it defines as farmland 'which has the soil quality, growing season, and moisture supply needed to produce economically sustained high yields of crops when treated and managed according to acceptable farming methods.'

short_description: State-level opposition to wind and solar projects through prohibitions.
long_description: Opposition to renewable energy facilities, particularly wind and solar projects, has been expressed in Illinois through state-level prohibitions. These measures have been adopted over the period 2019-2020.

short_description: Illinois enacted Public Law 102-1123 to limit local authority over renewable energy projects, including moratoriums and setback requirements.
long_description: On January 27, 2023, Illinois enacted Public Law 102-1123 which sets limits on counties' authority to restrict or otherwise regulate renewable energy facilities. The law prohibits counties from establishing moratoriums on wind or solar projects and establishes statewide setback parameters that override more restrictive local regulations.

short_description: Christian County adopted zoning code amendments with restrictive setback and shadow flicker requirements, effectively banning wind farms.
long_description: In September 2020, the Christian County Board voted to approve zoning code amendments that included restrictive setbacks and shadow flicker limits. The regulations were interpreted as effectively banning wind farms in the county. Following the adoption of Public Act 102-1123 (2023), the ordinance was revised to provide that if any restrictions were judicially determined to violate state law, then the limits set out in PA 102-1123 would apply.

short_description: DeKalb County passed an ordinance with strict setback, noise, and shadow flicker requirements for wind projects.
long_description: In 2018, DeKalb County passed an ordinance that required wind turbines to be set back from property lines by a distance of six times the turbine height and three miles from any municipality. The ordinance also required zero shadow flicker beyond property lines and limited background noise increases to no more than five dBA. These restrictions were later removed to achieve compliance with Public Act 102-1123 (2023).

short_description: Ford County imposed a moratorium on wind projects and later increased setback requirements.
long_description: In 2017, Ford County imposed a moratorium on wind energy projects while it revised its ordinance. In 2018, the county board’s zoning committee recommended increasing the existing 1,000-foot setback from buildings to 2,250 feet. At a hearing in October 2018, a group called Ford County Citizens for Property Rights demanded 3,250-foot setbacks from any property lines. On September 13, 2021, the County Board adopted an amended wind ordinance that increased setback to 2,250 feet from property lines upon which a primary structure is located.

short_description: Lee County imposed a moratorium on solar, wind, and battery storage projects.
long_description: In December 2021, the Lee County Board imposed a six-month moratorium on solar, wind, and battery storage projects. The moratorium was ultimately extended to November 2022. This type of moratorium would be invalid under state law pursuant to Public Act 102-1123 (2023).

short_description: Monroe County updated its zoning codes for wind and solar projects with increased setback limits, noise restrictions, and shadow flicker prohibitions.
long_description: In January 2021, the Monroe County Board updated its zoning codes for wind and solar energy systems. Among other changes, the new wind code increased setback limits to 2,640 feet from non-participating property lines; set noise limits of 30 and 35 dBA, depending on the time of day; and forbade any shadow flicker on neighboring properties and public roadways. This ordinance is likely invalid under state law pursuant to Public Act 102-1123 (2023).

short_description: Piatt County imposed a moratorium on wind energy project applications.
long_description: In August 2020, Piatt County extended a moratorium on wind energy project applications until March 2021 with unanimous approval from the County Board. In January 2023, Piatt County again imposed a moratorium on applications for wind energy projects through September 2023. This moratorium is likely invalid under state law pursuant to Public Act 102-1123 (2023).

short_description: Tazewell County approved a six-month moratorium on new wind energy projects.
long_description: On July 27, 2022, the Tazewell County Board voted to approve a six-month moratorium on new wind energy projects until a new ordinance is adopted. The moratorium was adopted in response to a request from an organization called United Citizens of Tazewell County, LLC. This type of moratorium would be invalid under state law pursuant to Public Act 102-1123 (2023).

short_description: The Village of Teutopolis banned the construction of wind farms within its corporate limits and extraterritorial jurisdictional limits.
long_description: In June 2023, the Village of Teutopolis in Effingham County banned the construction of wind farms within the village’s corporate limits and extraterritorial jurisdictional limits.

short_description: Residents of Mercer County opposed a proposed solar farm, leading to the denial of a conditional use permit.
long_description: Mercer County residents have expressed opposition to a 380-acre solar farm that Birch Creek Energy has proposed for Alexis, Illinois. At an October 2023 meeting with the Mercer County Zoning Board, some residents expressed concerns about loss of farmland. Local opposition also focused on concerns about noise and environmental impacts, including impacts to endangered species. The Mercer County Zoning Board denied Birch Creek’s conditional use permit application in November 2023.

short_description: The Alta Wind Farm faced local opposition and legal challenges but eventually began operation in 2023.
long_description: The 200-MW Alta Wind Farm was approved in July 2020 by the DeWitt County Board despite local opposition. The project had been proposed nearly 10 years before. In October 2020, opponents filed two separate lawsuits to stop the project but dropped both of those lawsuits in March 2021. In July 2021, the DeWitt County Board approved a motion preventing the issuance of new building permits to Enel Green Power for the Alta Wind Farm until the company could prove that its turbines could be curtailed during severe weather events. An Illinois judge then issued a mandamus order holding that the Dewitt County Board lacked legal authority to halt the issuance of building permits. The wind farm proceeded to operation in June 2023.

short_description: Allen County, Indiana, prohibits wind energy conversion systems with specific characteristics.
long_description: According to the Allen County zoning ordinance, last updated in September 2019, wind energy conversion systems are prohibited if they have a nameplate capacity of more than 50 kW, a total height of more than 60 feet, or a total swept area of more than 40 feet.

short_description: Boone County, Indiana, adopted a 2-year moratorium on large-scale renewable energy projects.
long_description: In April 2024, the Boone County Board of Commissioners adopted a new 2-year moratorium on large-scale solar, wind, and storage projects. This followed local opposition to potential development in the area.

project_or_policy_name: Clark County Unified Development Ordinance (amended Nov. 2024)
short_description: Clark County, Indiana, imposed new requirements and a cap on solar projects.
long_description: In November 2024, the Clark County Commission issued new requirements for solar projects. The County has imposed a cap of 4,000 acres of ‘fenced area’ that can be devoted to solar in the county. The county increased setback requirements from neighboring residential dwellings.

short_description: Clinton County, Indiana, upheld a moratorium on wind farms.
long_description: Clinton County, Indiana, upheld a moratorium on wind farms in September 2019. This followed local opposition to potential development in the area.

short_description: Delaware County, Indiana, adopted a moratorium and increased setbacks for solar projects.
long_description: On February 22, 2022, the Delaware County Commissioners approved amendments to the County’s solar ordinance, including increasing the setback from neighboring property lines to 200 feet. The County Commissioners also enacted a 1-year moratorium on solar farm development; in August 2023, this was extended through the end of 2023.

short_description: Fulton County, Indiana, prohibits wind farms in unincorporated areas.
long_description: According to the Fulton County zoning ordinance, last updated in October 2018, wind farms are prohibited in all unincorporated areas of Fulton County. Previously, they were banned in all areas of the County.

short_description: Hamilton County, Indiana, set height and setback limits for wind turbines and prohibited solar projects on prime agricultural soils.
long_description: Under the Unified Development Ordinance of 2022, wind turbines must not exceed 300 feet in height and must be set back by at least 1.5 times the tower height from property lines; commercial solar projects are prohibited on prime agricultural soils and must be set back at least 300 feet from neighboring houses.

short_description: Henry County, Indiana, established buffer zones for wind projects.
long_description: As of April 2019, twelve of the fifteen towns within Henry County had passed resolutions establishing buffer zones where no wind projects could be built. These buffers extend approximately 4 miles around each town. The law voided any such ordinances or resolutions adopted after December 31, 2018.

short_description: Howard County, Indiana, increased setbacks and noise limits for wind turbines.
long_description: In 2015, Howard County adopted amendments to a wind ordinance that increased setback requirements from 1,500 feet to 2,000 feet from the nearest property and decreased the noise limit from 50 dBA to 40 dBA.

short_description: Jasper County, Indiana, established setbacks for wind and solar projects.
long_description: In January 2019, Jasper County adopted a 60-day moratorium on permits for large-scale solar projects, which was extended by 90 days in March 2019. The county’s zoning ordinance, last updated in January 2022, only allows commercial solar as an exceptional use in heavy industrial districts and disallows commercial solar in all other districts.

short_description: Kosciusko County, Indiana, adopted a moratorium on large-scale solar projects.
long_description: In January 2019, Kosciusko County adopted a 60-day moratorium on permits for large-scale solar projects, which was extended by 90 days in March 2019. The county’s zoning ordinance only allows commercial solar as an exceptional use in heavy industrial districts and disallows commercial solar in all other districts.

short_description: Lake County, Indiana, disallows ground-mounted solar as a primary land use.
long_description: Lake County’s solar ordinance, passed in April 2016, disallows ground-mounted solar as a primary land use throughout the county. Ground-mounted solar is permitted only as an accessory use throughout the county.

short_description: Madison County, Indiana, imposed a moratorium on new wind and solar projects.
long_description: In March 2024, the Madison County Board of Commissioners passed a resolution imposing an indefinite moratorium on all new wind farm projects with the stated intent of reviewing the county’s wind ordinance within a year. The December 2023 ordinance also requires solar farms to be set back 3 miles from waterways and other solar farms.

short_description: Marshall County, Indiana, banned all commercial wind development.
long_description: In or around 2013, Marshall County commissioners voted unanimously to ban all commercial wind development. The prohibition remains in effect as of the latest version of the zoning ordinance available online in February 2023.

short_description: Miami County, Indiana, increased setbacks for wind turbines.
long_description: In 2018, Miami County increased wind turbine setbacks to 2,000 feet from property lines and roadways amidst local opposition to a proposed 75-turbine project. Under the 2021 version of the ordinance, wind turbines must be set back 0.5 miles from rivers or reservoirs.

short_description: Montgomery County, Indiana, set setbacks for wind and solar projects.
long_description: A 2019 Zoning Ordinance in Montgomery County, Indiana, set setbacks for both wind and solar projects. The specific details of the ordinance are not provided here.

short_description: Adams County adopted wind regulations capping total turbines and setting setbacks.
long_description: In September 2024, Adams County adopted wind regulations that cap the total number of wind turbines in the county to 225 and require turbines to be set back at least 1.5 times their height from property lines.

short_description: Adair County capped the number of commercial wind turbines at 535, with existing turbines already in place.
long_description: In November 2019, Adair County’s Board of Supervisors capped the number of commercial wind turbines allowed in the county at 535. At that time, there were already 532 turbines either built or under construction.

short_description: Butler County’s zoning ordinance includes restrictions on wind development, including setbacks and noise limits.
long_description: Last amended in November 2022, Butler County’s zoning ordinance for unincorporated areas includes a number of restrictions on wind development. Commercial wind turbines must be set back 1,640 feet from participating property lines and 1,800 feet from non-participating property lines. They must also remain below 40 dBa.

short_description: Cerro Gordo County passed a moratorium on utility-scale solar, wind and storage systems.
long_description: In May 2023, the Cerro Gordo County Board of Supervisors passed a 15-month moratorium on utility-scale solar and wind energy, along with battery storage facilities. In December 2024, they voted unanimously to pass a moratorium on the installation of new utility-scale solar, wind, and battery-energy storage systems located on land zoned for agricultural use.

county: Pottawattamie County - City of Council Bluffs
short_description: Council Bluffs has prohibited wind energy conversion systems since 2009.
long_description: Since 2009, wind energy conversion systems, such as wind turbines and windmills, have been prohibited within the City of Council Bluffs.

short_description: Clinton County issued a three-month moratorium on commercial wind farm applications and extended it to June 2025.
long_description: On September 24, 2024, Clinton County’s Planning and Zoning Commission issued a three-month moratorium on commercial wind farm applications as they revised the county’s 2008 wind ordinance. This moratorium was extended in December 2024 and will run through June 2025. A community opposition group has been active in public hearings regarding the proposed ordinance.

short_description: Dallas County’s zoning ordinance limits wind turbine noise and sets setbacks.
long_description: The county zoning ordinance provides that noise from wind turbines cannot exceed 30 dBA for any period of time when measured from any dwelling, school, hospital, church, or public library existing at the time of approval. The ordinance further requires that turbines be set back at least 2,640 feet from property lines, residences, and other structures.

short_description: Emmet County approved a temporary moratorium on wind energy project permits.
long_description: In October 2024, the Emmet County Board of Supervisors approved a temporary moratorium on construction permits for new wind energy projects through January 2025 to give the Board time to update the county’s wind ordinance. The moratorium was extended in January 2025 for another six months.

short_description: Floyd County instituted a moratorium on utility-scale wind and battery storage projects.
long_description: On November 20, 2023, Floyd County instituted a moratorium on applications for utility-scale wind and battery storage projects, which was scheduled to run until May 20, 2024.

short_description: Greene County implemented a moratorium on utility-scale solar farms.
long_description: In March 2022, Greene County put in place a moratorium on utility-scale solar farms for either 6 months or until the Iowa legislature passes a law that addresses solar farms. The moratorium was adopted following a public hearing at which residents spoke out against a proposed project by National Grid Renewables.

short_description: Grundy County passed an indefinite moratorium on wind farm construction and new regulations with setback requirements.
long_description: In May 2021, the Grundy County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 to pass an indefinite moratorium on wind farm construction in the county. In 2023, the County passed new wind regulations, including a setback requirement of 5 times turbine height from non-participating dwellings.

short_description: Hardin County implemented an indefinite moratorium on wind farms.
long_description: An indefinite moratorium on wind farms was implemented in the fall of 2019.

short_description: Henry County approved a one-year moratorium on rezoning for commercial wind energy.
long_description: In April 2024, the Henry County Board of Supervisors approved a 1-year moratorium on the rezoning of land for commercial wind energy or other forms of alternative energy generation.

short_description: Humboldt County adopted a one-year moratorium on new energy systems.
long_description: In January 2024, Humboldt County adopted a 1-year moratorium on new energy systems, including commercial wind, solar, and transmission systems.

short_description: Johnson County approved a temporary moratorium on utility-scale solar energy farms.
long_description: In December 2021, the Johnson County Board of Supervisors approved a temporary moratorium on the issuance of conditional use permits for utility-scale solar energy farms with a cumulative nameplate alternating current capacity greater than 10 MW. The Board set the moratorium to expire in June 2022.

short_description: Kossuth County adopted a nine-month ban on large-scale solar farm applications.
long_description: In October 2024, the Kossuth County Board of Supervisors adopted a 9-month ban on the processing of large-scale or utility-scale solar farm applications.

short_description: Linn County adopted a moratorium on utility-scale solar installations.
long_description: In October 2022, Linn County adopted a moratorium on utility-scale solar installations. The moratorium has since been extended multiple times and was last set to expire on September 30, 2023.

short_description: Governor Laura Kelly continued the Tallgrass Heartland Wind Moratorium in July 2020, which protects parts of 12 counties.
long_description: In 2004, Governor Kathleen Sebelius instated a wind development moratorium on parts of the Flint Hills to protect the tallgrass prairie. In 2011, Governor Sam Brownback expanded and renamed it as 'Tallgrass Heartland.' This moratorium was continued by Governor Laura Kelly in July 2020.

short_description: Barton County adopted a temporary moratorium on commercial solar projects and updated zoning regulations to include a 'no build' zone around Cheyenne Bottoms.
long_description: In May 2023, the Barton County Commission voted for a temporary moratorium on commercial solar projects until the end of the year. In March 2024, they approved an amendment updating zoning regulations to include a 'no build' zone around Cheyenne Bottoms.

short_description: Brown County adopted a moratorium on wind energy facility permitting to work on zoning regulations.
long_description: In July 2022, Brown County adopted a moratorium on wind energy facility permitting in order to work on zoning regulations. The duration of the moratorium is unclear.

short_description: Cherokee County adopted a wind energy ordinance with setback and noise restrictions.
long_description: In August 2021, Cherokee County adopted a 1-year moratorium on wind energy development. In October 2022, the county commissioners adopted an ordinance limiting turbine height to 440 feet at the highest blade, setting a 39 dBa noise limit during the evening, and establishing a 5,250-foot setback requirement from the nearest property line.

project_or_policy_name: Douglas County Wind Energy Moratorium and Solar Ordinance
short_description: Douglas County adopted a wind energy moratorium and increased setbacks for solar projects.
long_description: In December 2013, the Douglas County Commission issued a moratorium on wind farm development that lasted until April 2014. In May 2024, the Commission voted to adopt new wind regulations increasing setbacks from property lines to 2,500 feet. The county adopted a solar ordinance in 2022 limiting cumulative solar farm acreage and requiring setbacks.

short_description: Franklin County adopted a moratorium on wind farm development in unincorporated areas.
long_description: In May 2023, the Franklin County Board of Commissioners approved an amendment to the Franklin County Zoning Regulations establishing a moratorium on planning, establishment, construction, application for, or permitting of special use permits for wind farms in unincorporated areas until December 31, 2026.

project_or_policy_name: Harvey County Wind and Solar Moratorium
short_description: Harvey County established a moratorium on commercial wind and solar projects and updated zoning regulations.
long_description: In February 2023, Harvey County Commission established a 6-month moratorium on commercial wind and solar projects. In November 2023, the Commission amended the Unified Development Code to prohibit commercial wind and utility-scale solar projects while allowing community solar projects of 10 acres or less.

short_description: Johnson County updated its solar farm ordinance to set a maximum area and buffer zone.
long_description: In June 2022, Johnson County updated its solar farm ordinance setting the maximum area for a solar project at 2,000 acres and requiring a 1.5-mile buffer from neighboring city limits.

short_description: Kearny County established setback and height limits for wind energy projects.
long_description: Wind energy conversion systems must be set back at least 2,000 feet from any property line. With the consent of neighboring landowners, this limit may be reduced to 1,000 feet. The maximum turbine height is 350 feet by default but can be increased to 400 feet if efficiency increases are shown.

short_description: Labette County refused to sign road agreements with industrial wind farm developers.
long_description: In March 2022, the Labette County Commission voted to refuse signing any road agreements with industrial wind farm developers in response to widespread opposition.

short_description: Leavenworth County adopted a wind energy ordinance with setback and height restrictions.
long_description: In August 2022, Leavenworth County adopted an ordinance setting a 1,500-foot setback from property lines and a 200-foot tower height limit for wind turbines.

short_description: Linn County enacted a permanent ban on commercial wind construction.
long_description: In July 2023, the Linn County Commission voted to permanently ban commercial wind construction. The county had previously extended its moratorium multiple times.

project_or_policy_name: McPherson County Wind and Solar Moratoriums
short_description: McPherson County indefinitely banned wind turbines and extended a moratorium on commercial solar projects.
long_description: In November 2018, McPherson County adopted an indefinite moratorium on conditional-use permits for the construction of wind turbines. In 2021, the county adopted a moratorium on commercial solar energy projects which it indefinitely extended in August 2023.

short_description: Nemaha County extended its wind energy moratorium for an additional year.
long_description: In May 2019, Nemaha County adopted a moratorium on wind energy projects. The moratorium was most recently extended for an additional 12 months in October 2023.

project_or_policy_name: Osage County Wind and Solar Ban
short_description: Osage County banned commercial wind and solar projects within its borders.
long_description: On October 24, 2022, the Osage County Commission unanimously adopted a measure to prohibit any new commercial wind and solar projects. The county allows only small systems of 30 kW or less for alternate energy development.

short_description: Pawnee County extended its moratorium on utility-scale commercial solar projects for three years.
long_description: In the fall of 2022, the Pawnee County Commission enacted a 1-year moratorium on utility-scale commercial solar projects. In November 2023, they voted to extend this moratorium by an additional 3 years.

policy_mechanism: setback, height limit with resident permission
short_description: Prairie County established setback and height limits for wind energy projects with resident permission.
long_description: Zoning regulations require that wind turbines be set back 2,500 feet from active residential buildings. The setback can be reduced to 1,000 feet with written permission of all affected residents.

short_description: Reno County banned wind development in all zoned areas.
long_description: In December 2021, the Reno County Commission banned wind development in all zoned areas.

short_description: Wind turbines must be set back at least 1,000 feet from property lines and at least 2,000 feet from residential neighborhoods, schools, hospitals, or nursing homes.
long_description: Under House Bill 291 of 2014, adopted in 2014, wind turbines must be set back at least 1,000 feet from property lines and at least 2,000 feet from residential neighborhoods, schools, hospitals, or nursing homes.

project_or_policy_name: Prohibition on ground-mounted solar panel systems in agricultural districts
short_description: Prohibits ground-mounted solar panel systems from being the primary use of a property in an agricultural district if the property is smaller than ten acres.
long_description: Boyle County, Kentucky, prohibits ground-mounted solar panel systems from being the primary use of a property in an agricultural district if the property is smaller than ten acres.

project_or_policy_name: Solar ordinance for large-scale solar projects
short_description: Requires that certain large-scale solar projects be set back at least 1,000 feet from any lot line and at least 2,000 feet from the nearest lot line of any property containing a residential use or quasi-public use.
long_description: Hopkinsville’s solar ordinance requires that certain large-scale solar projects be set back at least 1,000 feet from any lot line and at least 2,000 feet from the nearest lot line of any property containing a residential use or quasi-public use.

project_or_policy_name: Solar ordinance for large-scale solar projects
short_description: Establishes a 2,000-foot setback for large-scale solar projects from any non-participating property line and any right-of-way for a publicly maintained roadway or rail-line.
long_description: Lyon County passed a solar ordinance that establishes a 2,000-foot setback for large-scale solar projects from any non-participating property line and any right-of-way for a publicly maintained roadway or rail-line. This was adopted on May 8, 2024.

project_or_policy_name: Solar ordinance for utility-scale solar projects
short_description: Utility-scale solar projects must be set back at least 500 feet from private property lines, and at least 600 or 750 feet from dwellings, schools, and many other occupied buildings, depending on the size of the property.
long_description: Mason County’s solar ordinance mandates that utility-scale solar projects be set back at least 500 feet from private property lines, and at least 600 or 750 feet from dwellings, schools, and many other occupied buildings, depending on the size of the property. This was adopted on April 19, 2023.

project_or_policy_name: Solar ordinance for large-scale solar projects
short_description: No more than 2,000 acres in the unincorporated areas of the county may be used for large-scale solar projects.
long_description: Meade County’s solar ordinance mandates that no more than 2,000 acres in the unincorporated areas of the county may be used for “Level 3” (large scale) solar. This was adopted on May 24, 2021.

project_or_policy_name: Banning commercial solar projects and restricting visibility of solar panels on flat roofs in non-residential zones
short_description: Bans commercial solar projects and requires that solar panels on flat roofs in non-residential zones not be visible from public rights-of-way, parking lots, and adjacent properties.
long_description: Villa Hills has banned commercial solar projects by requiring in its solar ordinance that the primary purpose of solar energy systems be for providing power for the property where the system is located, rather than for commercial use. It also requires that solar panels on flat roofs in non-residential zones not be visible from public rights-of-way, parking lots, and adjacent properties. This was adopted on November 30, 2022.

short_description: Duke Energy Renewables announced its intent to discontinue pursuing the construction of a wind farm in Mason and Fleming Counties due to local opposition.
long_description: In May 2014, Duke Energy Renewables announced its intent to discontinue pursuing the construction of a wind farm in Mason and Fleming Counties. The project, which would have included 26 to 100 wind turbines, had encountered local opposition, and the developer explained in a letter that it concluded the project had little chance of success.

short_description: Clark County Fiscal Court denied two ordinances that would have expanded the places solar farms could be zoned in the county, leading to a victory for an anti-solar community group.
long_description: In August 2021, amidst Geenex Solar’s early planning of a large-scale solar project in Clark County, the Clark County Fiscal Court denied two ordinances that would have expanded the places solar farms could be zoned in the county. The Clark CoaliDon, an anti-solar community group, celebrated the decision as a victory.

short_description: Hardin County Planning Commission denied a conditional use permit for Hardin Solar LLC, with almost 200 residents attending the commission meeting and many belonging to Hardin County Citizens for Responsible Solar.
long_description: In January 2022, the Hardin County Planning Commission denied a conditional use permit for Hardin Solar LLC. Almost 200 Hardin County residents attended the commission meeting, many of them belonging to Hardin County CiDzens for Responsible Solar. This group is opposed to industrial solar projects and has claimed credit for the denial of Hardin Solar’s permit.

short_description: Local residents collected signatures opposing a 100-MW, 1,100-acre solar farm in Madison County on the grounds that it would be an eyesore and harm property values.
long_description: Local residents collected 387 signatures for a petition opposing a 100-MW, 1,100-acre solar farm in Madison County on the grounds that it would be an eyesore and harm property values. However, in December 2020 or January 2021, the Madison County Board of Adjustments approved the project.

project_or_policy_name: NextEra’s Mason County Wind Energy Project
short_description: NextEra Energy Resources announced it was abandoning research on a potential wind project in Mason County due to state restrictions and anticipated local restrictions, including increased setbacks.
long_description: In May 2014, NextEra Energy Resources submitted a letter to Mason County officials announcing that it was abandoning research on a potential wind project in the county due to state restrictions and anticipated local restrictions, including increased setbacks.

short_description: Mercer County Fiscal Court denied approval for a 1,200-acre solar project proposed by Savion, overriding the recommendation of the county’s planning and zoning commission.
long_description: In October 2020, the Mercer County Fiscal Court denied approval for a 1,200-acre solar project proposed by Savion, overriding the recommendaDon of the county’s planning and zoning commission. Opponents organized against the project on a Facebook group called “Preserve Mercer County Farm Land” and spoke at a public meeting in August 2020.

short_description: Hardin County Commission denied a request to change the zoning of 1,030 acres from rural residential to industrial for the development of the Stonefield Solar Project. A lawsuit was filed challenging the permitting of the solar project in a heavy industrial zone.
long_description: In May 2023, the Hardin County Commission denied a request by participating landowners to change the zoning of 1,030 acres from rural residential to industrial to allow for the development of the Stonfield Solar Project. The Harden Fiscal Court eventually approved the zoning change in July 2023. Later that month, a citizen’s group called Hardin County Citizens for Responsible Solar filed a lawsuit challenging the permitting of the solar project in a heavy industrial zone, arguing that the project does not qualify as manufacturing and is at odds with the Hardin County Comprehensive Plan.

short_description: A January 2020 ordinance prohibits wind turbines within 3 miles of any business or residence in unincorporated areas of Jefferson Davis Parish.
long_description: Under a January 2020 ordinance, no wind turbine may be installed within 3 miles of any business or residence in the unincorporated areas of Jefferson Davis Parish. The ordinance was enacted to address local concerns about visual impacts and other issues.

short_description: A moratorium on commercial solar farms was approved in August 2022 by the St. James Parish Council.
long_description: On August 17, 2022, the St. James Parish Council approved a moratorium through March 2023 on commercial solar farms. The moratorium was imposed shortly after D.E. Shaw Renewable Investments submitted a proposal to build a solar farm on 3,900 acres in the parish, which the planning commission rejected. Local residents advocating for the moratorium expressed concerns about visual impacts.

short_description: A moratorium on solar farms was established in March 2021 and extended until new regulations were passed in April 2022.
long_description: In March 2021, Washington Parish established a moratorium on solar farms as it sought to develop a regulatory ordinance. The moratorium was extended several times, until the Washington Parish Council passed new regulations on solar projects in April 2022.

short_description: A lawsuit was filed against the Calcasieu Parish zoning board and police jury in September 2021 over a proposed solar farm.
long_description: In September 2021, local residents of Southeast Calcasieu Parish filed a lawsuit against the parish zoning board and police jury to contest the approval of a 3,400-acre solar farm that would generate 300 to 400 MW. Opponents of the project stated that they have not received sufficient guarantees as to human health and safety, as well as impacts on birds and other wildlife. On November 19, 2024, the Calcasieu Planning and Zoning Board rejected a zoning exception necessary for construction to proceed.

short_description: A land use permit for a proposed solar farm was denied by the St. James Parish Council in June 2024.
long_description: In June 2024, after more than 2.5 hours of comments at a public meeting, the St. James Parish Council denied by 4-3 vote a land use permit for St. James Solar, a 2,200-acre, 360-MW solar farm proposed by D.E. Shaw Renewable Investments (DESRI). The Council’s denial followed the St. James Parish Planning Commission’s 8-1 rejection of the project in April 2024. DESRI had agreed to offer a $4.67 million community benefits package and stated that the solar farm would have extensive buffers, fencing, and screening such that it would be virtually invisible and noiseless to passerby. The project, however, would have required a special exception from the agricultural and residential land use designations in the land use plan, which prohibit solar farms, and that exception was denied.

short_description: A proposed solar farm faces opposition from residents citing concerns about property devaluation and loss of farmland.
long_description: Developer NextEra has proposed a 2,057-acre solar project in Iberville and Pointe Coupee Parishes. Pointe Coupee Parish residents have generally not opposed the project, but a contingent in Iberville Parish has stood in strong opposition to it. Citing concerns about devalued property, loss of farmland, and impacts to the parishes’ rural atmosphere, project opponents held up signs saying “no solar” and “you’re not wanted here” at a September 2023 parish meeting. Parish President Mitchell Ourso voiced his opposition to the project, saying, ‘I cannot support this project here in our parish. . . . Before there was industry in our parish, everything was agriculture. This has no economic impact, and I think it can be detrimental for years to come in White Castle.’

short_description: Governor Janet Mills signed L.D. 1619, which banned offshore wind projects in Maine state waters and imposed a moratorium on large-scale solar projects.
long_description: In July 2021, Governor Janet Mills signed into law L.D. 1619, sponsored by Senator Mark Lawrence. The law permanently banned the development of all offshore wind projects in Maine state waters but allowed the permitting of offshore wind in federal waters if the Governor’s Energy Office developed a planned research strategy for such projects by March 2023. It also created the Offshore Wind Research Consortium (ORWC) to study the effects of offshore wind energy on the Gulf of Maine.

short_description: City Council imposed a moratorium for up to 180 days on solar projects due to aesthetic concerns.
long_description: In August 2021, after residents voiced aesthetic concerns about utility-scale solar projects, the City Council of Augusta (Kennebec County) imposed a moratorium for up to 180 days on solar projects.

short_description: City Council adopted a 6-month moratorium on large-scale solar projects.
long_description: In August 2023, the Brewer city council (Penobscot County) adopted a 6-month moratorium on large-scale solar projects.

short_description: City Council enacted a 6-month moratorium on solar development due to concerns about overdevelopment.
long_description: On October 18, 2021, citing concerns about overdevelopment, the Ellsworth City Council (Hancock County) enacted a 6-month moratorium on solar development. The moratorium was ultimately extended until October 13, 2022.

short_description: Residents voted to adopt a new ordinance requiring solar projects to be set back 300 feet and impose a moratorium on utility lines.
long_description: In March 2023, residents of the town of Albion (Kennebec County) voted at a Town Meeting to adopt a new ordinance that requires solar projects to be set back 300 feet from roads or residential buildings. In August 2023, Albion residents voted to impose a 6-month moratorium on utility lines and corridors in response to the Aroostook Renewable Gateway Project.

short_description: Town passed a 180-day moratorium on large-scale solar facilities due to water contamination and wildlife concerns.
long_description: In March 2024, the Town of Athens (Somerset County) passed a 180-day moratorium on large-scale solar facilities, citing potential for water contamination as well as wildlife concerns.

short_description: Town extended a moratorium on wind and solar projects to draft new ordinances.
