long_description: A moratorium on wind and solar projects that went into effect in August 2020 was extended multiple times as the town developed new ordinances for wind and solar energy. Under the new solar ordinance adopted in November 2022, no more than 10 acres of wooded land may be cleared for a solar project, and solar arrays must not exceed 12 feet in height.

short_description: Town imposed a 180-day moratorium on commercial solar projects.
long_description: In March 2022, the Town of Corinth (Penobscot County) imposed a 180-day moratorium on commercial solar projects.

short_description: Town imposed a moratorium on solar facilities to draft amendments to its Land Use Ordinance.
long_description: In February 2024, the Town of Cutler (Washington County) imposed a moratorium on solar facilities, citing additional time to draft amendments to its Land Use Ordinance to accommodate solar facilities. The moratorium was extended until August 2025.

short_description: Town Council passed a 180-day moratorium on commercial solar arrays.
long_description: In May 2024, the Town Council of Dexter (Penobscot County) passed a 180-day moratorium on commercial solar arrays.

short_description: Town Council passed a wind ordinance requiring setbacks from non-participating residences.
long_description: In September 2015, the Fort Fairfield Town Council (Aroostook County) passed a wind ordinance requiring a 1-mile setback from all non-participating properties.

short_description: Town enacted a wind turbine ordinance with setback and noise limits.
long_description: In November 2015, the Town of Freedom (Waldo County) enacted a wind turbine ordinance that requires all wind turbines to be set back from scenic or special resources. Depending on the height and megawatt capacity of the turbine, it must be set back either 1.5 times, 3 times, or 13 times the turbine height from non-participating landowners. Shadow flicker is limited to ten hours per year, and noise is limited to between 30 and 40 dBa.

short_description: Town imposed a moratorium on commercial solar facilities and banned larger projects.
long_description: In April 2021, the Town of Glenburn (Penobscot County) imposed a 2-month moratorium on commercial solar facilities. Then, in March 2022, Glenburn banned solar facilities larger than 15,000 square feet.

short_description: Town adopted an amendment limiting the size of solar projects to 15 acres, effectively killing a proposed project.
long_description: In November 2024, the Town of Greene (Androscoggin County) voted overwhelmingly to adopt an amendment limiting the size of any solar project to 15 acres. This amendment effectively killed a 600-acre solar project proposed by Swift Current Energy.
Maryland’s highest court held in 2019 that state law preempts local zoning authority approval for the siting and local of generating stations such as solar energy generating systems.

short_description: Allegany County requires wind turbines to be set back 2,000 feet from residences and 5,000 feet from schools.
long_description: The Allegany County ordinance mandates a setback of 2,000 feet for wind turbines from residences and 5,000 feet from schools.

short_description: Anne Arundel County prohibits large-scale wind energy projects in any zoning district.
long_description: County officials have stated that large-scale wind energy projects are not permitted in any zoning district within Anne Arundel County.

policy_mechanism: moratorium, setback, height restriction, buffer zone
short_description: Carroll County adopted a 6-month moratorium on community solar farm applications and amended its land use ordinance to increase restrictions on commercial solar projects.
long_description: In March 2023, Carroll County adopted a 6-month moratorium on applications for community solar farms on agricultural land. In December 2024, the county amended its land use ordinance to restrict commercial solar projects in residential and commercial districts, set height limits, and require vegetative buffers.

short_description: Harford County amended its Environmental Land Preservation program to protect agricultural land from renewable development.
long_description: The Harford County Council amended the Environmental Land Preservation program in February 2024, allowing the county to spend up to $7 million to prevent renewable development on high-value farmland and offer each landowner up to $3,000 per acre.

short_description: Somerset County explicitly prohibits wind energy systems as a principal use of land.
long_description: The Somerset County Zoning Ordinance, last updated in August 2019, explicitly prohibits the use of wind energy systems on any land within the county.

short_description: Worcester County prohibits large wind energy conversion systems with a capacity greater than 100 kW in any district.
long_description: Since June 15, 2015 or earlier, Worcester County regulations prohibit the installation of large wind energy conversion systems with a capacity greater than 100 kW in any zoning district within the county.

short_description: Montgomery County Planning Board submitted comments opposing a 4-MW community solar project in the Agricultural Reserve zone.
long_description: Chaberton Energy filed an application for a 4-MW community solar project in Montgomery County’s Agricultural Reserve zone. The Planning Board opposed the project, citing conflicts with local zoning requirements and received over 140 letters and emails from residents opposing it.

short_description: Worcester County Commissioners rescinded the denial of a 4-MW solar farm proposal after an administrative hearing and appeal.
long_description: The Worcester County Commissioners rescinded their previous denial of a 30-acre, 4-MW solar farm proposal by Chaberton Snow Solar LLC. The rescission followed an administrative hearing and appeal to the Worcester County Circuit Court in December 2023.

short_description: Local residents organized a group to oppose the Dan’s Mountain Wind Farm project, which faced legal challenges.
long_description: The proposed 17-turbine Dan’s Mountain Wind Farm in Allegany County has faced opposition from local residents who formed the Allegany Neighbors and Citizens for Home Owners Rights (ANCHOR) group. The project was challenged legally by ANCHOR, and the Court of Special Appeals upheld the approval.

project_or_policy_name: Georgetown University’s Charles County Solar Project
short_description: Local environmental groups opposed a 32.5-MW solar project due to potential ecological impacts.
long_description: Environmental groups raised opposition to Georgetown University’s Charles County Solar Project, citing concerns over species and ecosystem impacts. The Maryland Department of the Environment denied a permit for the project in August 2019.

short_description: Local governments and environmental groups oppose a high-voltage transmission line project.
long_description: The proposed Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project by PSEG encountered opposition from local governments in Baltimore, Carroll, and Frederick counties, as well as the Maryland Farm Bureau and an organization called Stop MPRP. The opponents are soliciting comments against the project and working to block approval.

project_or_policy_name: Mills Branch Wind and Solar Project
short_description: Local opposition continued after the project was converted from wind to solar.
long_description: Apex Clean Energy announced in April 2015 that they were slowing the application process for a proposed 5,000-acre Mill Branch Wind Farm due to local opposition. The developer eventually decided to convert the project to a solar energy project, but faced ongoing local opposition until January 2017 when the Public Service Commission denied the certificate of public convenience and necessity.

short_description: Local opposition to a 27.5 MW solar project due to forest clearing.
long_description: Origis Energy USA proposed the Ripley Road Solar Project, which required clearing 190 acres of forest and was conditionally approved by the Public Service Commission. However, in August 2019, the Maryland Department of the Environment denied a wetlands permit for the project.

short_description: Supreme Judicial Court struck down Waltham's zoning restrictions on large-scale solar energy systems.
long_description: The City of Waltham’s zoning code effectively limited large-scale solar energy facilities to industrial zones. The building inspector denied permission for a 1-MW solar facility based on local zoning restrictions, which were subsequently struck down by the Supreme Judicial Court in June 2022.

short_description: Residents of Charlton voted to cap the number of large-scale solar installations in town.
long_description: In 2019, residents of the Town of Charlton voted at a town meeting to cap the number of large-scale solar installations at 30 total, thus prohibiting new projects. This followed a one-year moratorium imposed in 2018.

short_description: Residents of Northfield voted for a one-year moratorium on utility-scale solar projects and battery storage facilities.
long_description: In May 2024, residents of the Town of Northfield voted in favor of two citizen’s petitions to place a one-year moratorium on utility-scale solar projects and battery storage facilities. The moratoriums were intended to provide time for drafting bylaws regulating these installations.

short_description: Pelham amended its solar and energy storage bylaws to require setbacks and forestland conservation.
long_description: In May 2023, Pelham residents voted to amend the town’s solar and energy storage bylaws. The town prohibited energy storage systems as a principal use in all zoning districts and required large-scale solar projects (1.5-15 acres) to be set back at least 500 feet from nearby streets. Developers were also required to set aside four times the total area of a solar installation for forestland conservation.

short_description: Shutesbury’s solar bylaw prohibits solar plants larger than fifteen acres.
long_description: Shutesbury’s solar bylaw, adopted in May 2008 and amended in June 2021, prohibited solar plants larger than fifteen acres. In January 2023, residents voted to adopt a revised town bylaw for solar arrays that would have banned energy storage systems as a principal use in all zoning districts and limited large-scale solar installations (1.5-15 acres) to special use in Forest Conservation Districts. The Massachusetts Attorney General’s office disapproved of the January 2023 bylaw, resulting in the pre-2023 bylaw regaining legal effect. A lawsuit filed by developer PureSky Energy challenged the town's solar regulations.

project_or_policy_name: SunEdison 2.4-MW solar array on a capped town landfill
short_description: Lawsuit against town officials for allegedly violating an agreement with the state.
long_description: In 2011, the Town of Amherst selected SunEdison to build a 2.4-MW solar array on a capped town landfill. Citizens filed a lawsuit against town officials in response, alleging that they violated an agreement with the state requiring the site be used for recreational purposes. The lawsuit became moot when the state legislature passed a bill allowing all capped municipal landfills to serve as sites for solar projects. In April 2012, plaintiffs amended the lawsuit to include potential impacts on grasshopper sparrow habitat. The lawsuit was dismissed without prejudice in December 2015 and terminated by town officials in July 2016.

short_description: Developer withdrew application for solar farm as Town Council considered moratorium.
long_description: In November 2021, ASD Shutesbury MA Solar LLC withdrew an application to build a 11-MW solar farm in Amherst as the Town Council considered enacting an 18-month moratorium on large solar arrays.

short_description: Planning Board rejected proposed Bullard Farm Solar Plant due to health concerns.
long_description: The Holliston Planning Board unanimously rejected the proposed Bullard Farm Solar Plant in 2012. A local group claimed that the solar array would pose risks to the health of area residents due to toxic chemicals in the panels and the output of electromagnetic frequency.

short_description: Developer abandoned project after years of legal challenges and delays.
long_description: In 2017, the developer of Cape Wind, a proposed 454-MW offshore wind farm, abandoned the project after spending $100 million of his own money. The project faced opposition from groups such as the Alliance to Protect Nantucket Sound, fishing groups, and Native American tribes. Legal challenges delayed the project, leading two utilities to cancel their contracts with Cape Wind in 2015.

short_description: Developer terminated power purchase agreements and withdrew authorization for host community agreement.
long_description: In December 2022, developer Avangrid requested to terminate power purchase agreements for the Commonwealth Wind project. The agreements were formally terminated in October 2023. In response, the Barnstable Town Council unanimously voted to withdraw authorization for negotiation of a host community agreement for the project. The town manager expressed reservations about the draft environmental impact report.

short_description: Michigan has state-level restrictions on wind and solar projects.
long_description: Michigan has enacted laws that prohibit or restrict the development of wind and solar energy projects, reflecting opposition to renewable energy facilities within the state.

short_description: Adams Township imposed a 6-month moratorium on commercial wind and solar projects.
long_description: In August 2021, the Adams Township Board unanimously voted to impose a 6-month moratorium on commercial wind and solar projects. The vote came at a time when Adams was being considered as the site for a wind farm.

short_description: Almer Township adopted a wind ordinance requiring setbacks and noise limits.
long_description: In 2020, Almer Township adopted a wind ordinance requiring that commercial wind turbines be set back from property lines by a distance of 4 times the height of the highest blade tip. It further limits noise to 39 dBA at night and limits shadow flicker on neighboring properties to zero.

short_description: Arcadia Township’s 2019 zoning ordinance limits noise and establishes setbacks for wind turbines.
long_description: Arcadia Township’s 2019 zoning ordinance for wind energy limits noise to 40 dBa and establishes setbacks from property lines, occupied buildings, and rights-of-way of 1,640 feet for turbines less than 500 feet and 3.28 times turbine max blade tip height for turbines greater than 500 feet.

short_description: Augusta Township adopted a 6-month moratorium on large solar energy systems.
long_description: In March 2022, Augusta Township adopted a 6-month moratorium on large solar energy systems, subject to renewal.

short_description: Batavia Township approved a wind ordinance limiting the height of turbines.
long_description: The Batavia Township Board approved a restrictive wind ordinance in September 2020 that limits the height of wind turbines to 330 feet. The restrictions were promoted aggressively on Facebook by a group called Concerned Citizens of Branch County in response to efforts by DTE Energy to develop a wind farm in the area.

short_description: Beaver Township adopted restrictions on wind and solar energy.
long_description: In May 2018, Beaver Township adopted restrictions on wind energy amidst opposition to DTE Energy’s plans to develop a wind farm in the area. As of October 2022, the township’s zoning ordinance requires that wind turbines be set back at least 1,760 feet from property lines or 4 times tower height, whichever is greater, and limits shadow flicker to zero; it also limits the height of commercial solar energy systems to 12 feet and requires that they be set back 500 feet from property lines.

short_description: Bedford Township only allows solar development in industrial-zoned districts.
long_description: As of September 2021, Bedford Township only allowed solar development in industrial-zoned districts, excluding it from agricultural districts.

short_description: Berlin Charter Township disallows solar development in agricultural-zoned districts.
long_description: Berlin Charter Township’s zoning code, last amended in February 2020, disallows solar development in agricultural-zoned districts and limits it to a special use in industrial-zoned districts.

short_description: Bridgehampton Township initially proposed a wind moratorium but eventually rejected it.
long_description: In March 2016, a Bridgehampton Township council member moved for a wind moratorium, but this moratorium was eventually rejected. In November 2016, the township adopted a six-month moratorium on new wind development under a new board supervisor.

short_description: Casnovia Township adopted wind energy restrictions similar to Almer Township.
long_description: In October 2019, Casnovia Township adopted wind energy restrictions that are virtually identical to those of Almer Township. The ordinance requires that commercial wind turbines be set back from property lines by a distance of 4 times blade tip height. It further limits noise to 39 dBA at night and limits shadow flicker on neighboring properties to zero.

short_description: Claybanks Township established restrictions for wind turbines.
long_description: Claybanks Township’s 2019 zoning ordinance establishes the following restrictions for wind turbines: setbacks of 1,500 feet from the nearest inhabited structure on a participating property and 3,000 feet from the nearest non-participating property line; a turbine max blade tip height limitation of 500 feet; and a noise limit of 40 dBa at non-participating properties.

short_description: Clinton County established a moratorium on utility-scale wind and solar projects.
long_description: In May 2023, the Clinton County Board of Commissioners established a 1-year moratorium on wind power plants and large-scale solar energy facilities. In April 2024, the Clinton County Board passed multiple amendments restricting utility-scale wind energy, including: a minimum setback from non-participating properties of 1,600 feet or 4 times turbine height, whichever is greater; a maximum turbine height of 450 feet; no shadow flicker on non-participating properties; and a noise limit of 45 dBA.

short_description: Cohoctah Township adopted a moratorium on utility-scale solar projects.
long_description: In December 2021, Cohoctah Township adopted a year-long moratorium on utility-scale solar. The township adopted another year-long utility-scale solar moratorium in February 2023.

short_description: Conway Township adopted a moratorium on commercial wind and solar projects.
long_description: In April 2023, Conway Township adopted a year-long moratorium on commercial wind and solar projects.

short_description: Southwest Michigan Solar Project sued Decatur Township after voters rejected an ordinance allowing the project.
long_description: In August 2023, Southwest Michigan Solar Project sued Decatur Township after voters in a special election rejected an ordinance that would have allowed the project to proceed. The developers allege that the governing 2022 ordinance had a misprint in the zoning district abbreviations that resulted in the ordinance inadvertently disallowing the project. A new ordinance was adopted to correct the mistake, but 80% of residents voted it down in a special election.

short_description: State-level ban on wind energy projects in certain counties.
long_description: The state of Minnesota has implemented a ban on new wind energy projects in specific counties, effective from 2019 to 2020. This restriction is aimed at addressing local concerns and environmental impacts.

short_description: Minnesota passed a law that preempts local zoning rules for large energy storage, wind, and other electric generating facilities.
long_description: In May 2024, Governor Walz signed the Minnesota Energy Infrastructure Permiung Act, which consolidated permiung requirements and eased transmission siting while limiting circumstances under which environmental impact statements and certificates of need are required. This act preempts local zoning, building, or land use rules for large energy storage systems with a capacity of 10 MW or more, wind facilities of 5 MW or more, and other electric generating facilities of 50 MW or more.

project_or_policy_name: 1-year moratorium on wind and solar energy conversion systems
short_description: Chippewa County adopted a 1-year moratorium on wind and solar projects to study possible ordinance reforms.
long_description: In February 2024, Chippewa County Commissioners adopted a 1-year moratorium on the permitting or zoning of wind and solar energy conversion systems in order to study possible ordinance reforms.

project_or_policy_name: Moratorium on solar projects in agricultural preserve areas
short_description: Minnetrista implemented a moratorium on solar projects in agricultural areas, which was later lifted.
long_description: In October 2020, the City of Minnetrista (Hennepin County) implemented a moratorium on the construction of solar projects in agricultural preserve areas. In May 2021, the moratorium was lifted when the city adopted a new ordinance that caps all ground systems at 3,000 square feet and allows solar systems only as an accessory use.

short_description: Scandia approved a 1-year moratorium on solar projects due to visual impacts from an existing farm.
long_description: In April 2022, the Scandia City Council in Washington County approved a 1-year moratorium on the installation of any solar energy systems. This was partly in response to residents' displeasure with the visual impacts of a solar farm that was developed in 2016. Following the moratorium, the town amended its zoning laws to increase setbacks for solar projects.

project_or_policy_name: 1-year moratorium on solar and wind energy systems
short_description: Meeker County approved a 1-year moratorium on solar and wind projects to consider updates to zoning ordinances.
long_description: In February 2024, the Meeker County Commissioners voted 4-1 to approve a 1-year moratorium on solar and wind energy systems in order to consider updates to the county’s wind and solar zoning ordinances.

short_description: Traverse County passed an interim ordinance temporarily prohibiting wind projects for 12 months, extended by another 12 months.
long_description: In 2023, Traverse County passed an interim ordinance that temporarily prohibited the permitting and construction of wind energy facilities for 12 months. In February 2024, the county extended its moratorium by an additional 12 months to allow time to update its current Wind Energy Conversion Systems ordinance.

project_or_policy_name: 1-year moratorium on 5-acre community solar gardens in agricultural areas
short_description: Wright County implemented a 1-year moratorium on community solar gardens in agricultural areas.
long_description: In 2021, Wright County implemented a 1-year moratorium on 5-acre community solar gardens in agricultural areas. The county subsequently adopted new restrictions requiring a 1-mile separation between solar gardens.

short_description: Big Blue Wind Farm faced noise complaints and a PUC intervention, leading to ongoing issues.
long_description: The Big Blue Wind Farm in Faribault County is an 18-turbine, 36-MW wind farm that went online in December 2012. Ager years of complaints about noise, the Public Utilities Commission (PUC) intervened in 2017 and discovered that the project’s noise protocol had never been approved. Residents then pushed for the farm to be completely shut down, but the PUC instead ordered the developer to address the problems and issued a warning.

short_description: McLeod County rejected a solar garden proposal on prime farmland, overturned by the Court of Appeals.
long_description: The McLeod County Board of Commissioners rejected a proposal for a 3.5-acre solar garden on prime farmland in 2021. In 2024, the Minnesota Court of Appeals overturned the County Board’s decision, finding that their stated concerns about impacts to neighboring property values and prime farmland were arbitrary and capricious and ordered the Board to approve the project.

short_description: Marshall Solar Project faced local opposition but was ultimately approved by the PUC.
long_description: The Marshall Solar Project in southwestern Minnesota is a 500-acre, 62-MW solar energy complex that faced opposition from local residents who argued it would lower property values and disrupt their rural lifestyle. Opponents also complained that the developer had not sought out non-prime farmland for the project. The Public Utilities Commission (PUC) unanimously approved the project in March 2016.

short_description: Minnetrista rejected a proposed solar farm and implemented a moratorium on solar projects.
long_description: A proposed solar energy system on 5-6 acres of vacant land in Minnetrista, Hennepin County, initially earned the Planning Commission’s recommendation for approval in September 2020. However, after receiving public comment, the city council rejected the project in October 2020 and implemented a moratorium on solar energy projects while it revised its ordinance to make clear that only small accessory-use systems are allowed.

short_description: New Era Wind Farm was denied further authorization by the PUC due to risks to endangered bird species.
long_description: A drawn-out battle between New Era Wind and Goodhue County residents led to the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission (MPUC) voting against further authorization of the New Era Wind Farm in August 2013. The MPUC determined that the operation of this wind farm would pose a risk to eagles and other endangered bird species in Goodhue County. New Era Wind announced it was terminating its plans for the project soon after.

short_description: Residents opposed a proposed 396-MW solar farm and 70-MW battery storage facility in Hinds County, Mississippi.
long_description: In 2021, Apex Clean Energy began acquiring leases for a proposed 6,000-acre, 396-MW solar farm and 70-MW battery storage facility. Nearby residents organized opposition through a letter to the Hinds County Planning and Zoning Department and a Change.org petition with over 1,000 signatures. The Hinds County Planning Commission voted against recommending the project; however, the Hinds County Board of Supervisors approved it in June 2024.

short_description: Residents in Lamar County opposed a proposed 90-MW solar farm, raising concerns about property values and agricultural land.
long_description: In July 2023, residents organized a community meeting to express opposition to the proposed 90-MW, 1,700-acre Minkar solar farm. Two residents created signs, an online petition, and a social media group in opposition to the project; as of February 2024, the petition had 336 signatures. The Lamar County Board of Supervisors will ultimately decide on whether to approve the project.

short_description: Boone County approved new wind regulations preventing turbines within 1,750 feet of residential property and setting a maximum turbine height.
long_description: In November 2021, the Boone County Commission in Missouri approved new wind regulations that prevent turbines from being constructed within 1,750 feet of residential property and set a maximum turbine height of 263 feet. The regulations further restrict commercial scale wind turbines to industrial zoning districts.

short_description: Buchanan County banned commercial wind turbines citing property devaluation, noise, and quality of life concerns.
long_description: In March 2020, the Buchanan County Commission in Missouri banned commercial wind turbines due to concerns about property devaluation, noise, and effects on quality of life. The ban was adopted without any public support for allowing such projects.

short_description: New Bloomfield adopted new solar farm regulations prohibiting them within 1,000 feet of city limits.
long_description: On April 27, 2022, the City of New Bloomfield in Callaway County, Missouri, adopted new regulations for solar farms that prohibit such projects within 1,000 feet of city limits. This was a response to a developer’s proposal for a 100-MW facility on 600 acres.

short_description: Clinton County passed a moratorium on wind development.
long_description: In 2016, Clinton County commissioners in Missouri passed a moratorium on wind development. The latest version of the Clinton County Zoning and Subdivision Order, last amended July 19, 2019, prohibits Commercial Wind Energy Conversion Systems within the county.

short_description: Monroe County implemented an 18-month moratorium on wind energy development.
long_description: In August 2019, the Monroe County Board of Commissioners in Missouri put in place an 18-month moratorium on wind energy development amidst early plans for a wind energy project in the county.

project_or_policy_name: Grain Belt Express Tiger Connector Expansion
short_description: Residents and agricultural groups opposed the Grain Belt Express Tiger Connector Expansion, but it was eventually approved.
long_description: A Facebook group with 600 followers called “Callaway County Missouri Solar Invasion” organized residents to oppose a 40-mile connector to the 800-mile Grain Belt Express (GBX) transmission line. Opponents raised concerns about visual impacts and loss of farmland caused by the solar projects that the transmission line will support. In October 2024, the state’s court of appeals ruled that Chariton County government could not block the construction of the project by refusing permission to cross its county roads.

short_description: The Guthrie Solar Project was rendered a nuisance by new local regulations.
long_description: The regulaDons described above that the City of New Bloomfield adopted on April 27, 2022, rendered plans for the 100-MW, 600-acre Guthrie Solar Project a nuisance. The project was planned to be within city limits, and the new rules prohibited any commercial solar project within 1,000 feet of city limits.

short_description: The Osborn Wind Project faced local opposition and lawsuits, with a settlement allowing up to 24 turbines.
long_description: The 200-MW, 97-turbine Osborn Wind Project was proposed in Clinton and DeKalb Counties in 2010. Local residents founded the Concerned Citizens for the Future of Clinton and DeKalb Counties group to oppose wind development. Following a number of lawsuits, NextEra and the Washington Township Zoning Commission reached a settlement agreement in 2018 that allowed for the construction of up to 24 turbines. The developer dropped a lawsuit against Clinton County in 2020.

short_description: Wibaux County adopted zoning rules to restrict wind development, including a setback of 1,250 feet from property lines and 1.5 miles from residences.
long_description: On October 23, 2024, Wibaux County in Montana became the first county to adopt countywide zoning to restrict wind development. The new rules require wind turbines to be set back 1,250 feet from property lines and 1.5 miles from residences. These rules were adopted as part of an effort to block AES’s proposal for a 235-MW Wibaux Wind Farm with 50 MW of battery storage.

short_description: FX Solutions' application for a special use permit to build the Basin Creek Solar Project was denied by the BuWe-Silver Bow Zoning Board of Adjustment in July 2021. The company appealed the decision.
long_description: On July 15, 2021, the BuWe-Silver Bow Zoning Board of Adjustment denied a permit to FX Solutions for the Basin Creek Solar Project on 1,600 acres. In August 2021, FX Solutions appealed the decision. The company argued that the Zoning Board erred by focusing only on public opposition and ignoring support for the project.

short_description: PaWern Energy's Crazy Mountain Wind Project was abandoned after a judge issued a preliminary injunction in March 2019, making it impossible to obtain necessary financing.
long_description: PaWern Energy proposed a 22-turbine wind project in Sweet Grass County. Four companies that owned neighboring land initiated legal action alleging nuisance. In March 2019, a Montana judge issued a preliminary injunction on construction while the case awaited trial. By July 2019, PaWern asserted that the preliminary injunction made it impossible to obtain necessary financing and satisfy contractual obligations, leading to the abandonment of the project.

short_description: Local residents formed Friends of Mission Creek to oppose Sagebrush Energy's proposed 11-turbine wind farm, citing landscape and golden eagle concerns.
long_description: In 2010, Sagebrush Energy proposed an 11-turbine wind farm east of Livingston, Montana. Local residents formed the Friends of Mission Creek group to halt the project due to concerns about impacts on the natural landscape and local populations of golden eagles. The project appears to have stalled shortly thereafter.

short_description: GreenHunter Energy's proposed 500-MW wind farm in Valley County was abandoned after facing opposition from environmental groups and local residents.
long_description: In 2005, GreenHunter Energy proposed a 500-MW wind farm in a remote area north of Glasgow, Montana. In 2007, the company abandoned the project due to opposition from the Montana Wilderness Association, Montana Audubon Society, and the Montana Wilderness Society, who raised concerns about impacts on a nearby wilderness area.

short_description: Adams County adopted resolutions requiring wind turbines to be set back from neighboring dwelling units and prohibiting concentrated solar power.
long_description: In 2018, Adams County required that wind turbines be set back 2,400 feet from neighboring dwelling units and 6,000 feet from any existing wind turbine not owned by the applicant. In 2019, a resolution prohibited concentrated solar power facilities but allowed photovoltaics with proper permits.

short_description: Brown County's zoning regulations require commercial wind turbines to be set back from property lines and roads.
long_description: As of May 2020, Brown County’s Zoning Regulations required that commercial wind turbines be set back 1 mile from property lines and roads.

short_description: Buffalo County adopted new setback requirements for wind turbines.
long_description: In March 2023, the Buffalo County Commissioners adopted new setback requirements for wind turbines that require distances of 2 miles from any burial site or the Platte River; 3 miles from any agriculture residential zoned property; 3 miles from property lines of nonparticipating properties; 3 miles from any church, hospital, pool, or park; and 5 miles from any village or city.

short_description: Burt County adopted new zoning regulations for wind turbines.
long_description: In December 2024, the Burt County Board of Supervisors adopted new zoning regulations that require commercial wind turbines to be set back 3 miles from any towns or villages, 1 mile from property lines, and 0.5 miles from any occupied dwelling. The ordinance further limits the number of turbines in the county to a cumulative total of 20 turbines, prohibits shadow flicker on roads, and provides that noise shall not exceed 40 dBA from any dwelling on a nonparticipating property, except during periods of severe weather.

short_description: Cedar County's zoning ordinance requires commercial wind turbines to be set back from nonparticipating dwelling units, public conservation lands, and existing commercial wind turbines.
long_description: Cedar County’s zoning ordinance, last updated in June 2022, requires commercial wind turbines to be set back at least one mile from non-participating dwelling units, public conservaDon lands, and other existing commercial wind turbines not owned by the applicant.

short_description: Gretna City Council approved a temporary moratorium on solar plants and associated facilities.
long_description: In July 2020, Gretna City Council approved a temporary moratorium on solar plants and associated facilities through October 2020 or until city codes were updated, whichever was sooner.

short_description: Dakota County amended its zoning regulations to require wind turbines to be set back from neighboring dwelling units and wetlands.
long_description: On July 26, 2021, Dakota County amended its zoning regulations to require that commercial wind turbines be set back 2 miles from neighboring dwelling units (up from 2,700 feet) and 2 miles from wetlands and other conservation lands (up from 600 feet).

short_description: Dawson County adopted a 1-year moratorium on wind farm applications and amended its regulations to impose new setbacks.
long_description: In November 2022, Dawson County adopted a 1-year moratorium on wind farm applications. In May 2023, the Dawson County Board of Commissioners adopted amendments to its wind regulations that impose setbacks of 3 miles from non-participating property lines, participating dwellings, road rights-of-way, and public conservation lands. The regulations also limit noise to 40 dBa at the nearest dwelling.

short_description: Franklin Township implemented regulations requiring wind turbines to be set back from public roads and nonparticipating private property lines.
long_description: In September 2015, Franklin Township implemented regulations requiring that wind turbines be set back 1,640 feet from public roads and non-participating private property lines. The regulations were dragged by a group called Bohemian Alps Wind Watchers and implemented around the same time by five other townships in Butler County.

project_or_policy_name: Board of Zoning Appeals' Resolution 2020-07-16 and 2023-03-23
short_description: Gage County adopted a moratorium on new permits for wind farms and banned commercial wind turbines within 1 mile of property lines.
long_description: In July 2020, Gage County adopted a 3-month moratorium on new permits for wind farms. In November 2021, Gage County adopted amendments that banned commercial wind turbines within 1 mile of property lines of non-participating property owners, a major change from the 2019 zoning regulations, which required only that turbines be set back from property lines by a distance of 2 times turbine height. Gage County subsequently imposed an indefinite moratorium on commercial solar facilities in 2022 to halt solar development while considering new solar restrictions.

short_description: Greeley County adopted a 3-year moratorium on renewable energy applications.
long_description: In April 2024, the Greeley County Board of Commissioners adopted a 3-year moratorium on renewable energy applications.

short_description: Hamilton County's zoning ordinance requires wind turbines to be set back from property lines of nonparticipating landowners.
long_description: An ordinance last amended in 2019 requires that wind turbines be set back 2 miles from property lines of non-participating landowners.

short_description: Holt County amended its zoning ordinance to require wind turbines to be set back from neighboring dwelling units.
long_description: Holt County amended its zoning ordinance in November 2022 to require commercial wind turbines to be set back at least 1 mile from neighboring dwelling units.

short_description: Kearney County's zoning ordinance requires solar facilities to maintain noise limits and set back from nonparticipating properties.
long_description: KEARNEY COUNTY, NEB., ZONING REGULATIONS § 7.42(12) require turbines to be set back 1 mile from incorporated towns, schools, churches, state-owned recreational areas, and the homes of any non-participating landowners.

short_description: Lancaster County's zoning code sets noise limits and setback requirements for wind turbines.
long_description: In 2015, Lancaster County adopted updates to its zoning code requiring wind turbines maintain noise limits of 40 dBa in the day and 37 dBa at night at non-participating dwellings. The county also set the following setback requirements: 2 times turbine height from non-participating property lines, 3.5 times turbine height from non-participating dwellings.

project_or_policy_name: Nye County Moratorium on Renewable Energy Permits
short_description: Nye County approved a temporary 6-month moratorium on processing permits for renewable energy generation facilities.
long_description: In November 2022, the Nye County Board of County Commissioners approved a temporary 6-month moratorium on processing permits for renewable energy generation facilities. In January 2025, the moratorium expired and a new ordinance took effect which implements a setback requirement of 1 mile for solar systems from residentially zoned property.

short_description: The Biden Administration's creation of a new national monument in the Mojave Desert appears to have derailed plans for the 400-MW Angora Solar Project.
long_description: On March 21, 2023, the Biden Administration announced the creation of a 450,000-acre Avi Kwa Ame National Monument in the Mojave Desert along the border between California and Nevada to protect an area important to certain Native American tribes. This designation, actively sought by conservation groups, local government officials, and tribal leaders, appears to have derailed plans for the 400-MW Angora Solar Project, which is currently proposed to be built on 2,000 acres within the proposed monument. The developer asked the administration for a carve-out, but it was apparently not granted.

short_description: Arevia Power withdrew its application to construct the 850-MW Bajle Born Solar project due to opposition from groups like Save Our Mesa.
long_description: In July 2021, Arevia Power withdrew its application to construct the 850-MW BaWle Born Solar project on the Mormon Mesa in the desert north of Las Vegas. The project would have been the largest ever built in the United States and faced opposition from groups such as Save Our Mesa, who raised concerns about visual impacts and tourism impacts.

project_capacity_mw: 800 MW solar + up to 800 MW storage
short_description: The Bureau of Land Management sided with local opponents and gave the BeaWy Energy Center Project low priority status.
long_description: In June 2022, the Bureau of Land Management sided with local opponents of BeaWy Energy Center and two other large solar projects (Bonnie Clare Solar and Sawtooth Energy Center) near Death Valley National Park by giving them “low priority” permitting status. If approved, the projects would collectively generate 3,300 MW of electricity on up to 25,000 acres of land. The Bureau cited proximity to Death Valley National Park and sensitive habitat for the Mojave Desert tortoise as concerns. The projects are opposed by Nevada-based Basin and Range Watch, which thanked BLM for its decision.

project_capacity_mw: 1,500 MW solar + 1,000 MW DC-coupled storage + 500 MW AC-coupled storage
short_description: The Bureau of Land Management sided with local opponents and gave the Bonnie Clare Solar Project low priority status.
long_description: In June 2022, the Bureau of Land Management sided with local opponents of Bonnie Clare Solar Project and two other large solar projects (BeaWy Energy Center and Sawtooth Energy Center) near Death Valley National Park by giving them “low priority” permitting status. If approved, the projects would collectively generate 3,300 MW of electricity on up to 25,000 acres of land. The Bureau cited proximity to Death Valley National Park and sensitive habitat for the Mojave Desert tortoise as concerns. The projects are opposed by Nevada-based Basin and Range Watch, which thanked BLM for its decision.

short_description: Western Watersheds Projects sued the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Land Management, and National Park Service over their approval of large-scale solar development in Clark County.
long_description: In September 2023, the organization Western Watersheds Projects sued Secretary of the Interior Deb Haaland, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Land Management, and National Park Service over their approval of large-scale solar development in portions of Clark County that is home to the threatened Mojave Desert tortoise. The organization seeks relief under the Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act.

short_description: The Bureau of Land Management rejected an application by Eolus Vind to construct a 500-MW wind farm near Death Valley National Park.
long_description: In November 2018, the Bureau of Land Management rejected an application by Eolus Vind of Sweden to construct a 500-MW, 248-turbine wind farm on 32,531 acres of public land in Nevada. Documents obtained in response to a FOIA request appear to show that Assistant Secretary Joseph Balash decided to terminate the project after conversations with and receiving input from tribal groups, mining groups, fish and wildlife experts, and the military.

short_description: Ormat Nevada Inc. was approved to construct two 30-MW geothermal plants on federal land in Dixie Valley, but the project is being challenged by environmental groups.
long_description: In November 2021, Ormat Nevada Inc. was approved to construct two 30-MW geothermal plants on federal land in Dixie Valley. In December 2022, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service listed the Dixie Valley toad as endangered, prompting the Center for Biological Diversity and Fallon Paiute-Shoshone Tribe to sue the Bureau of Land Management over the project’s approval. In July 2023, the U.S. Department of the Interior announced that it would begin a new environmental analysis of the project in light of the Dixie Valley toad being listed as endangered, halting construction of the project until the completion of the environmental review.

short_description: Several local community members have expressed opposition to the scale of the project’s impact on the largely undeveloped land in Esmeralda County.
long_description: The proposed Esmeralda Seven project in Nevada would combine 7 projects aggregating to a total of 5.3 GW. Several local community members have expressed opposition to the scale of the project’s impact on the largely undeveloped land in the county.

short_description: The Supreme Court of Nevada upheld a lower court’s permanent injunction preventing the construction of a wind turbine on residential property.
long_description: In 2013, the Supreme Court of Nevada upheld a lower court's permanent injunction preventing the construction of a proposed wind turbine on residential property, holding that the turbine would create a nuisance.

short_description: The Burning Man Project and Friends of Nevada Wilderness sued the Bureau of Land Management to stop a geothermal exploration project.
long_description: On January 9, 2023, the Burning Man Project and Friends of Nevada Wilderness filed a lawsuit against the federal Bureau of Land Management to stop a geothermal exploration project. In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs allege that the noise, traffic, light, and drilling from the project would be inconsistent with the Burning Man Project’s use of the area during the annual Burning Man festival. On April 3, 2023, the Paiute Tribe of Nevada, Gerlach Preserves Society, and several local residents joined the lawsuit against the project. That same month, the Washoe County Commission voted to overturn a permit that the county had previously approved in January to allow the company to drill up to 13 test wells.

county: Various (Clark, Lyon, Esmeralda, Lyon, Mineral, and Nye)
short_description: The Greenlink West Transmission Project is facing opposition from conservation groups due to a stretch crossing through Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument.
long_description: A proposed 470-mile transmission line that would stretch from Las Vegas to Reno and carry up to 4,000 MW of renewable energy is facing opposition from conservation groups. Opponents of the plan, including the founder of Nevada-based Basin and Range Watch, have raised concerns about a 1.5-mile stretch that crosses through Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument, where shallowly buried fossils could be disturbed during construction. In May 2023, the Department of the Interior released a draft environmental impact statement for the project.

short_description: State banned offshore wind projects.
long_description: The state of New Hampshire enacted a ban on offshore wind projects in 2019-2020, prohibiting any development in state waters due to concerns over environmental and economic impacts.

project_or_policy_name: Ordinance for Large Wind Energy Systems
short_description: Town of Canaan approved an ordinance for large wind energy systems with specific height, setback, and shadow flicker requirements.
long_description: In March 2018, the Town of Canaan in Granon County approved an ordinance for large wind energy systems that sets a maximum turbine blade diameter height of 350 feet, establishes a setback requirement of three times the turbine blade diameter height, and mandates that shadow flicker cannot exceed eight hours per year in total. The ordinance includes other requirements.

short_description: Antrim Wind Project was approved by the New Hampshire Site Evaluation Committee in December 2016, despite opposition from project opponents.
long_description: In December 2016, the New Hampshire Site Evaluation Committee approved the 29-MW Antrim wind farm, which would involve nine wind turbines on a ridge. Project opponents, including local residents and environmental groups, appealed the decision to the New Hampshire Supreme Court. In May 2018, the court ruled against the project opponents on all counts, allowing the project to move forward. The project began commercial operations in 2019.

short_description: Franklin Solar Project was approved by the New Hampshire Supreme Court in April 2024, overturning a local Planning Board's denial.
long_description: In April 2024, the New Hampshire Supreme Court overturned the City of Franklin Planning Board’s denial of a 6-acre, 1-MW solar farm proposed by GSSG New Hampshire. The project met the city’s zoning ordinances but was opposed by residents concerned about disruptions to scenery and property values. The court stated that a board cannot deny projects that comply with zoning ordinances based solely on subjective views. The court essentially approved the project by issuing a builder's remedy which allows a project to proceed if it meets zoning ordinances.

short_description: Granite Reliable Wind Farm was proposed in 2010 and completed as planned in 2012, despite concerns from the Appalachian Mountain Club.
long_description: In 2010, a 99-MW, 33-turbine wind farm near Groveton was proposed. The Appalachian Mountain Club raised concerns that the project might impact sensitive high-elevated forest. However, the project was ultimately completed as originally planned in 2012.

short_description: Concord Solar Project was denied by the local zoning board and not pursued further.
long_description: In 2018, NextEra Energy’s plans for a 10-MW, 54-acre solar farm in Concord were rejected by the local zoning board because there would be too much 'impervious surface' for a residential open-space zoning lot. The zoning board denied the developer's request for rehearing.

short_description: Wild Meadows Wind Farm was abandoned in 2014 due to political and regulatory climate concerns.
long_description: The proposed 75.9-MW, 23-turbine Wild Meadows Wind Farm was abandoned in 2014. In a statement, the developer blamed 'the current political and regulatory climate' in New Hampshire for the project's cancellation. The project faced opposition from residents and local groups including the Appalachian Mountain Club.

short_description: New Jersey has enacted a ban on new wind and solar projects in certain areas.
long_description: In 2019, New Jersey passed legislation that prohibits the construction of new utility-scale wind and solar projects in specific coastal and agricultural regions. This ban is intended to protect sensitive ecosystems and farmland. Legal challenges have been filed against this policy by renewable energy developers.

short_description: Atlantic County Board of County Commissioners approved a nonbinding resolution calling for a moratorium on offshore wind development.
long_description: On February 21, 2023, the Atlantic County Board of County Commissioners in New Jersey approved a resolution calling on state and federal officials to impose a moratorium on offshore wind development until the cause of recent whale deaths could be determined. The resolution is nonbinding.

short_description: Middletown Township passed a nonbinding resolution calling for a moratorium on offshore wind projects.
long_description: On March 6, 2023, the township committee of Middletown Township in Monmouth County, New Jersey, passed a resolution calling on state and federal officials to impose a moratorium on offshore wind projects. Proponents cited recent whale deaths. The resolution is nonbinding.

short_description: Atlantic Shores South Project faced opposition from multiple municipalities and environmental groups, leading to lawsuits.
long_description: The Atlantic Shores South Project, a 2,800-MW offshore wind project, faced significant opposition. In July 2023, all of the municipalities of Long Beach Island filed a letter with the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) claiming that the project does not comply with NJDEP’s coastal zone management regulations and should be sited farther offshore to avoid impacts on state coastal resources. In April 2023, Save Long Beach Island filed a lawsuit against the federal government challenging authorizations for Atlantic Shores and other offshore wind projects; this lawsuit was dismissed in February 2024. In August 2023, MOVE ‘EM OUT, a New Jersey nonprofit organization devoted to preserving the state’s beaches, announced its opposition to the project, arguing that it would have detrimental impacts on New Jersey's southern shoreline ecology. The project, if approved, would build 200 wind turbines 9 miles off New Jersey's coast. In December 2023, eight municipalities filed a lawsuit in state court against the NJDEP, seeking a judgment that the project violates New Jersey coastal regulations.

short_description: Residents in Bedminster Township opposed a proposed solar array on a historic farm, leading to the project's cancellation.
long_description: Residents in Bedminster Township mounted organized opposition to a proposed 132-acre solar array on a historic farm. The project was argued to ruin the rural landscape. Opponents voiced concerns about the project on a Facebook page called Stop the Bedminster Solar Power Plant. The developer withdrew its proposal in 2016.

short_description: Residents in Sea Girt opposed a proposed offshore wind project citing health hazards and beach blockage.
long_description: When Governor Murphy visited the community to promote the Leading Light Wind Project, more than 100 people attended to oppose it. They claimed that the project is a health hazard and blocks the Sea Girt beach.

county: Atlantic, Cape May, Monmouth, Ocean Counties
project_or_policy_name: New York Bight Offshore Wind Area
short_description: Save Long Beach Island sued the Interior Department over designating offshore wind areas in New York Bight.
long_description: Save Long Beach Island sued the Interior Department’s Bureau of Ocean Energy Management for designating certain areas in the New York Bight as wind energy areas. The group argued that the Interior Department violated NEPA and ESA by failing to consider environmental impacts and consult with other agencies before acting. In March 2023, a federal judge dismissed the lawsuit but allowed plaintiffs to amend and refile their complaint.

short_description: Residents in Freehold Township opposed a proposed solar farm on farms, leading to its rejection.
long_description: In September 2022, the township of Freehold’s Planning Board rejected a request to install solar panels on a portion of farms in the community. The developer, NJ Solar 2000, had intended to install over 9,000 solar panels, which it asserted could have powered over 500 homes in Freehold.

short_description: Ocean Wind 1 faced opposition from local governments and protesters, leading to lawsuits and project cancellation.
long_description: The proposed 98-turbine, 1,100-MW Ocean Wind 1 project faced significant opposition. Local governments twice denied necessary approvals for the onshore components of the project, prompting the state Board of Public Utilities to bypass local approvals in September 2022 and February 2023. Various citizens groups opposed to offshore wind filed lawsuits against the developer Ørsted and the State of New Jersey, challenging tax subsidies and consistency with coastal management laws. In July 2023, Ocean City Mayor Jay Gillian installed anti-wind farm signs at beach entrances located 15 miles from the project. In August 2023, a state Superior Court granted a land easement to allow the project to bring underground power cables onshore in Ocean City. In October 2023, Cape May County and several environmental, fishing, and hospitality organizations filed a lawsuit against the Interior Department and Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, seeking to reverse approval of the project. The lawsuit included claims under various federal laws. Later in October 2023, Ørsted announced that it was ceasing development on Ocean Wind 1 along with another project—Ocean Wind 2—citing high inflation, rising interest rates, and supply chain bottlenecks. In December 2024, Cape May County ended its lawsuit on the basis that the project had been canceled.

project_or_policy_name: Six Flags Theme Park Solar Project
short_description: Local environmental organizations challenged Jackson Township’s approval of a solar array on Six Flags property.
long_description: In January 2017, several local environmental organizations challenged Jackson Township's approval of a 21-MW solar array on 67 acres owned by Six Flags Theme Parks, Inc. in Jackson Township. The plaintiffs alleged that municipal ordinances that allowed the project were invalid and sought to block it.

short_description: State-level opposition to wind and solar projects through prohibitions.
long_description: Opposition to renewable energy facilities, particularly wind and solar projects, has been expressed in New Mexico through state-level prohibitions. These restrictions have been adopted between 2019 and 2023, with ongoing legal challenges.

short_description: Chaves County Planning and Zoning Commission denied permits for two 5-MW community solar projects based on objections from neighbors.
long_description: On April 6, 2022, the Chaves County Planning and Zoning Commission voted not to recommend permits sought by Cenergy Power for two 5-MW community solar projects. Local residents expressed concerns about visual impacts, harm to property values, runoff into nearby rivers, destruction of wildlife habitats, and land use.

project_or_policy_name: Chaves Solar 2 LLC Community Solar Project
short_description: Roswell-Chaves County Exterritorial Zoning Commission denied a 5-MW community solar project based on objections from nearby property owners.
long_description: In October 2021, the Roswell-Chaves County Exterritorial Zoning Commission voted against a permit for a 5-MW community solar garden. The commission received three protest letters and comments from three other property owners who opposed the project due to concerns about radiation, toxic materials, dust, glare, noise, temperature effects, wildlife effects, and property devaluation. In November 2021, the developer and landowners filed an appeal.

project_or_policy_name: Energy Management Inc.’s Community Solar Project
short_description: Roswell-Chaves County Exterritorial Commission denied a community solar project proposed by Energy Management Inc. after hearing objections from residents.
long_description: In November 2022, the Roswell-Chaves County Extraterritorial Commission voted against a community solar project proposed by Energy Management Inc. (EMI) after hearing objections from residents.

short_description: Roswell-Chaves County Exterritorial Commission denied two community solar projects proposed by NextEra, each 5 MW or smaller, after hearing objections from residents.
long_description: In November 2022, the Roswell-Chaves County Extraterritorial Commission voted against two community solar projects proposed by NextEra, each 5 MW or smaller, after hearing objections from residents.

short_description: Residents established groups to oppose a 96-MW solar farm with a 48-MW battery storage facility in Santa Fe County, leading to an online petition and complaints.
long_description: The Rancho Viejo Solar Project, a 680-acre, 96-MW solar farm with a 2-acre, 48-MW battery storage facility proposed by AES, has faced resistance from the local community. Residents have established the Clean Energy Coalition for Santa Fe County and New Mexicans for Responsible Renewable Energy to fight against the project. The latter started an online petition directed at Santa Fe County, asking that officials either deny the project’s conditional use permit application or issue a moratorium and amend county codes before considering the project further. Residents have expressed distrust toward the company and argued that the county has failed to adequately engage the community. A resident submitted in August 2023 a Notice of Violation to Santa Fe County and filed in September 2023 a complaint with the New Mexico Attorney General, alleging that the County’s meetings with AES violated New Mexico’s Open Meetings Act. The County denied the allegations, and the Attorney General responded that no violations occurred. In August 2024, residents attended a county meeting at which AES presented a revised plan that sought to address the community's concerns.

short_description: Luna County Board postponed a decision on a proposed 97.5-MW solar project after hearing from many opponents.
long_description: A proposed 97.5-MW project on 620 acres of private land has encountered opposition at contentious public meetings. In January 2023, after hearing from many project opponents, the Luna County Board voted unanimously to postpone a decision on the application.

short_description: Multiple state-level policies have been enacted or proposed to restrict renewable energy projects, including wind, solar, storage, transmission, and hydro.
long_description: Between 2019 and 2023, New York has seen the implementation of several state-level restrictions on various types of renewable energy projects. These include bans or prohibitions on certain technologies such as wind, solar, storage, transmission, and hydro. Legal challenges have been a common feature in these policy developments.

short_description: New York state law restricts renewable energy projects on agricultural land and Native American territories.
long_description: The New York State Legislature adopted a law in 2023 directing the New York Power Authority (NYPA) to develop renewable energy projects, with restrictions that prohibit development on agricultural land unless it is an agrivoltaics project or on Native American territory without consent.

short_description: Cattaraugus County IDA implements a moratorium on new solar and wind projects.
long_description: In 2022, the Cattaraugus County Industrial Development Agency (IDA) voted to implement a 6-month moratorium on new solar energy applications. In July 2022, it approved a moratorium on wind farm development. The IDA extended its moratorium in July 2023 until the end of 2023.

short_description: Chautauqua County adopts a motion opposing wind farms and sends a letter urging noise restrictions.
long_description: In 2019, the Chautauqua County legislature approved a motion formally opposing the construction of wind farms along Lake Erie. In December of the same year, the county board of health sent a letter to municipal offices urging them to pass ordinances restricting industrial wind turbines.

short_description: Johnstown city council bans commercial solar arrays.
long_description: In June 2024, the Johnstown city council prohibited commercial solar arrays in a ban affecting 5 square miles of land in Fulton County.

short_description: Olean Common Council approves a 1-year moratorium on large-scale solar projects.
long_description: In May 2023, the Olean Common Council voted to approve a 1-year moratorium on all large-scale solar projects. The decision was based on the need to draft updated solar regulations and a comprehensive plan.

short_description: Niagara County mandates extended producer responsibility for solar panels.
long_description: In June 2021, Niagara County adopted a law mandating extended producer responsibility for solar panels and requiring developers to submit detailed recycling plans. As of October 23, 2023, most manufacturers remain out of compliance.

short_description: Clifton Park Town Board approves a 6-month moratorium on ground-mounted solar facilities.
long_description: In January 2021, the Clifton Park Town Board approved a 6-month moratorium on ground-mounted solar facilities with a capacity of 25 kW or more. The moratorium was supported by Friends of Clifton Park Open Space.

short_description: Clinton Town prohibits utility-scale wind projects.
long_description: Since 2019 or earlier, the Town of Clinton has prohibited utility-scale wind projects by requiring that any wind energy system facility's primary purpose be to provide power for the principal use of the lot on which it is located and not for commercial purposes.

short_description: Coxsackie Town restricts utility-scale solar development to commercial and industrial zones.
long_description: In 2019, the Town of Coxsackie enacted an ordinance that restricted utility-scale solar development to the town's commercial and industrial zones. A lawsuit challenging the ordinance was dismissed.

short_description: Dryden Town implements a moratorium on certain public utility installations, including solar facilities.
long_description: In July 2016, the Town of Dryden implemented a 6-month moratorium on certain types of public utility installations, including solar facilities.

short_description: Duanesburg Town adopts a solar moratorium to consider changes to the 2016 solar law.
long_description: In January 2020, the Town of Duanesburg adopted a 6-month moratorium on large-scale commercial solar energy development in order to consider changes to a 2016 solar law amid opposition to a proposed Eden Renewables project.

short_description: Enfield Town imposes a moratorium on commercial wind and solar projects.
long_description: The Town of Enfield imposed a moratorium on commercial wind and solar projects in 2017. In August 2019, the town rescinded the solar moratorium and extended the wind moratorium until November 2019.

short_description: Farmersville Town Board passes a wind energy facilities law with increased setbacks and noise limits.
long_description: In early 2020, the Farmersville Town Board passed a Wind Energy Facilities Law that doubled setback minimums to 3,000 feet from residences and property lines, decreased the maximum height of turbines from 600 feet to 455 feet, and set noise limits of 45 dBa and below. These amendments became law near the same time as a proposed Alle-Catt Wind Farm was being planned.

short_description: Florida Town Board amends regulations to prohibit utility-scale solar and wind development.
long_description: In November 2023, the Florida Town Board amended its regulations to prohibit utility-scale solar and wind development. The exact details of these amendments are not provided in the text.

short_description: State-level opposition to wind and solar projects through prohibitions.
long_description: North Carolina has faced state-level opposition to renewable energy projects, particularly wind and solar, through legislative bans or prohibitions. These measures were adopted in 2019-2020.

short_description: House Bill 589 / Senate Law 192 imposed a moratorium on wind energy facility permitting until the end of 2018.
long_description: In July 2017, House Bill 589 / Senate Law 192 was signed into law. The law included a moratorium on the permitting of wind energy facilities until the end of 2018 for the purpose of studying the impact of future wind energy development on military operations, training, and readiness.

short_description: Brunswick County Board of Commissioners approved a resolution opposing wind farms within 24 nautical miles of the coast.
long_description: In August 2021, the Brunswick County Board of Commissioners approved a resolution opposing wind farms within 24 nautical miles of the coast. The towns of Ocean Beach Isle and Sunset Beach and the Village of Bald Head Island passed similar resolutions. These are nonbinding.

short_description: Carteret County requires utility-scale wind turbines to be set back 1 mile from property lines and roads, limited to 275 feet in height.
long_description: According to an ordinance last updated in 2014, Carteret County requires that utility-scale wind turbines of at least 1 MW be set back 1 mile from property lines and roads and limited to 275 feet in height. The ordinance also imposes penalties if noise exceeds 35 dBa for more than 5 minutes at the property line.

short_description: Craven County requires wind turbines to be set back 1 mile from property lines and limits sound to 35 dBa at the property line.
long_description: A county wind ordinance last modified in July 2021 requires that wind turbines be set back 1 mile from property lines and provides that shadow flicker on non-participating properties is not permitted. The ordinance further limits sound to 35 dBa at the property line.

short_description: Currituck County adopted a moratorium on new solar farms in January 2017, which remained in place until January 2019.
long_description: Currituck County adopted a moratorium on new solar farms in January 2017, which remained in place until January 2019. The county’s March 2022 Unified Development Ordinance does not allow “solar arrays” or “large” wind energy facilities in any zoning district.

short_description: Herndon County Commissioners approved a temporary solar moratorium in October 2020.
long_description: Herndon County Commissioners unanimously approved a temporary solar moratorium in October 2020. The moratorium was enacted in response to local opposition to the proposal for development of a nearby solar farm.

short_description: Iredell County restricts wind turbines to 350 feet in height and limits noise to 30 dBa at the property line.
long_description: Iredell County restricts wind turbines to 350 feet in height and limits noise to 30 dBa at the property line.

short_description: Rowan County instituted a moratorium on large solar farms, which was extended twice.
long_description: In October 2019, Rowan County instituted a moratorium on large solar farms, set to expire in April 2020. It was extended twice. At the time of the most recent extension on October 5, 2020, it was set to expire on April 6, 2021.

short_description: Woodland Town Council approved a moratorium on all future solar projects in 2015.
long_description: In 2015, the Woodland Town Council approved a moratorium on all future solar projects in the midst of opposition to a project proposed by Strata Solar.

short_description: Surry County Supervisors rejected plans for a 20-MW solar farm that would have been situated across the street from a historic homestead.
long_description: On June 16, 2022, County Supervisors rejected plans for a 20-MW solar farm that would have been situated across the street from a historic 17th century homestead. The Surry County Planning Commission previously found that the proposal conflicted with the county’s 2040 Comprehensive Plan due to visual impacts on scenic and cultural resources and the county’s ordinance, which requires that solar projects “avoid important historic, archaeological or cultural sites.” Eight out of the ten residents who spoke at a public hearing advocated against the project.

short_description: Rowan County Commission denied a rezoning request for a 575-acre solar farm after months of opposition from residents.
long_description: In November 2021, residents in Rowan County successfully blocked the construction of a 575-acre solar farm after months of opposition. The Rowan County Commission voted 4-1 to deny a rezoning request by Birdseye Renewable that would have allowed progress to begin on the solar farm. The commissioners pointed to local community opposition as justification for their votes.

short_description: County commissioners voted unanimously to reject a request for rezoning to allow construction of a 58-MW, 600-acre solar project.
long_description: On April 18, 2022, county commissioners voted unanimously to reject Duke Energy’s request for rezoning to allow construction of a 58-MW, 600-acre solar project that would offset 50% of Wells Fargo’s electricity usage in the state. The county planning board previously recommended approval of the project, but the county decided to reject it after hearing from five residents who spoke out against it.

short_description: Rowan County Commission denied a conditional use permit for a 65-MW solar farm and imposed a six-month moratorium on ground-mounted solar development.
long_description: In 2019, CooperaDve Solar LLC proposed a 65-MW solar farm on 428 acres in Salisbury that was primarily zoned for agricultural use. A large number of residents strongly opposed the project and raised concerns about potential adverse impacts on property values, the surrounding environment, and wildlife. At a public hearing before the Rowan County Commission on September 16, 2019, the commissioners made clear that they were unlikely to approve the project, and the developer subsequently withdrew its application for a conditional-use permit. During that same hearing, the commissioners also voted to impose a six-month moratorium on ground-mounted solar development across the county.

short_description: Coastal Pine Solar filed a lawsuit after its application to build a 2,300-acre solar farm was denied by county commissioners.
long_description: In December 2022, Coastal Pine Solar filed a lawsuit after its application to build a 2,300-acre solar farm was denied unanimously by county commissioners in September 2022. The company claimed that the commissioners misapplied zoning ordinances based on generalized fears of solar farms. In response, the county filed an affidavit claiming its denial was based on its belief that the transmission line that would be connected to the solar farm could not safely handle the power generated. The county then filed a motion to dismiss, which was denied by the Superior Court. In June 2023, after several conferences between the parties, the court ordered the two sides to enter mediation to settle the dispute.

short_description: Yadkin County denied a conditional use permit for the Shady Grove Solar farm and the developer appealed the decision.
long_description: Yadkin County denied a conditional use permit for the Shady Grove Solar farm in October 2020. The solar farm, a joint venture between Silver Creek Energy and Pine Gate Renewables, would have produced 22 MW on 285 acres. Opponents testified at an evidentiary hearing about their concerns of flooding from the removal of trees, as well as impacts to water quality and tourism. The developer appealed the decision in November 2020.

short_description: Woodland Town Council imposed a moratorium on all future solar projects in 2015.
long_description: In 2015, the Woodland Town Council imposed a moratorium on all future solar projects after opposition to a project proposed by Strata Solar. The moratorium was cited as a response to constituents’ concern of being “completely surrounded by solar farms.”

project_or_policy_name: City of Grand Forks prohibition on wind energy systems
short_description: Grand Forks City prohibits commercial wind energy systems and adopted a 90-day moratorium on new wind farms, later extended.
long_description: The City of Grand Forks in North Dakota has prohibited the installation of wind energy systems that generate power as a commercial enterprise. Additionally, the city adopted a 90-day moratorium on the siting of new wind farms, which was later extended by 60 days. Previously, the county amended its zoning regulations to require a setback of 0.5 miles from any wind turbine to the nearest residence.

short_description: Grand Forks County adopted a 90-day moratorium on new wind farms, later extended by 60 days.
long_description: On April 25, 2023, Grand Forks County in North Dakota adopted a 90-day moratorium on the siting of new wind farms. This moratorium was later extended by 60 days to August 15, 2023.

project_or_policy_name: Banning new transmission lines for wind energy within 1 mile of the Missouri River and two lakes on the county’s western border
short_description: McLean County banned new transmission lines for wind energy within 1 mile of the Missouri River and two lakes.
long_description: In May 2020, McLean County in North Dakota banned the construction of new transmission lines for wind energy projects within one mile of the Missouri River and two lakes on the county’s western border. This ban impeded plans to connect new renewable energy projects to a coal-fired power plant slated for closure.

short_description: McLean County introduced a 2-year moratorium on solar development.
long_description: In August 2020, McLean County in North Dakota introduced a two-year moratorium on the development of new solar projects. This moratorium was intended to give the Coal Creek power plant an opportunity to avoid closure.

project_or_policy_name: 2,500 feet setback requirement for wind turbines from non-participating residences
short_description: McLean County's zoning ordinance requires a 2,500 feet setback for wind turbines from non-participating residences.
long_description: In May 2022, McLean County in North Dakota updated its zoning ordinance to require that wind turbines be set back at least 2,500 feet from any non-participating residence.

short_description: Mercer County adopted a 2-year moratorium on wind energy applications, blocking the Garrison Buje Wind Farm.
long_description: In May 2020, Mercer County in North Dakota adopted a two-year moratorium on wind energy development applications. This moratorium blocked the planned Garrison Buje Wind Farm project.

short_description: Stark County approved a 9-month moratorium on wind energy development.
long_description: In September 2021, the Stark County Board of Commissioners in North Dakota voted unanimously to approve a nine-month moratorium on any wind energy development in the county. This decision came as the City of Dickinson was considering a proposed wind farm by Marathon and One Energy. In July of the same year, the Commission withdrew the moratorium pursuant to court order and directed the county planning and zoning director to draft a new, lawful moratorium.
