short_description: Dickinson Wind applied for a conditional use permit to construct an 87-turbine, 150-MW wind farm in Stark County. Local residents and the Concerned Citizens of County opposed the project.
long_description: Dickinson Wind applied for a conditional use permit to construct an 87-turbine, 150-MW wind farm in Stark County. The project was opposed by local residents and the Concerned Citizens of County, who spoke against it in a March 2016 hearing before the Public Service Commission (PSC). Despite opposition, the PSC approved the project in June 2016.

short_description: NextEra's application to construct the Burke County Wind Project was rejected by the PSC due to proximity to wetlands and potential wildlife impacts.
long_description: In June 2019, the Public Service Commission (PSC) in North Dakota rejected NextEra’s application to construct the Burke County Wind Project. The project was controversial in the community, where the planning and zoning commission had voted against it before the county commissioners approved it. NextEra submitted a revised application for a 74-turbine, 200-MW wind farm called Northern Divide Wind, which the PSC approved in June 2021.

short_description: PNE Wind proposed a wind farm in Burleigh County, which was denied by the county and led to a recall of officials who supported the project.
long_description: PNE Wind proposed a 70-turbine wind farm in Burleigh County near Morton Township. The issue became highly divisive in the local community, leading to the denial of county land use permits in May 2019, and a vote to recall Burleigh County officials who supported the project in August 2019. Opponents organized an anti-wind organization, North Dakota Visionkeepers, to block the project.

short_description: Orion Renewable Energy Ground applied for a zoning permit for a wind farm in Billings County, which was denied by the county due to concerns over visibility and impacts on Theodore Roosevelt National Park.
long_description: Orion Renewable Energy Ground submiWed a zoning application for a 114-turbine, 383-MW project in Billings County. During a public hearing on the project, local residents expressed concerns over property devaluation, effects on local tourism, and impacts on the visual landscape. In particular, residents expressed concerns about turbine visibility from the Painted Canyon Visitor Center and other parts of Theodore Roosevelt National Park. The Billings County Commission denied the permit in November 2016.

adopted_or_event_date_text: April 2024 (denial of preliminary project area permit)
short_description: McLean County denied a zoning permit for the Coal Creek Wind Farm, a 400-MW wind farm proposed by a developer.
long_description: In April 2024, McLean County Commissioners in North Dakota denied a preliminary project area permit for the proposed Coal Creek Wind Farm. The developer and participating landowners appealed the decision, but the McLean County Board of Commissioners denied their appeal in June 2024. Residents speaking at the public hearing expressed divided opinions on the project.

short_description: McLean County denied a zoning permit for the Discovery Wind Farm proposed by Apex Clean Energy.
long_description: In April 2024, the McLean County Board of Commissioners in North Dakota denied a zoning permit for the Discovery Wind Farm, a 94-turbine wind farm proposed by Apex Clean Energy. The developer and participating landowners appealed the decision, but the McLean County Board of Commissioners denied their appeal in June 2024. Residents speaking at the public hearing expressed divided opinions on the project.

short_description: Capital Power proposed a wind farm in Mercer County, which was blocked by the moratorium passed by the county commissioners.
long_description: In 2018, Capital Power proposed a 152-MW wind farm in Mercer County. At a public hearing about the project, local residents expressed concern over the 'attack on coal,' an industry that employs many residents. In May 2020, the Mercer County Commission passed a moratorium on wind development that blocked the project.

short_description: Multiple bans and prohibitions on wind and solar projects have been enacted in Ohio.
long_description: Several counties in Ohio have passed local ordinances banning or prohibiting the installation of wind and solar energy facilities. These actions were part of a broader effort to restrict renewable energy development, with some opposition citing concerns over property values, aesthetics, and noise pollution.

short_description: H.B. 483 requires wind turbines to be at least 1,125 feet from the nearest property line.
long_description: Ohio House Bill 483 of 2014 mandates a setback requirement for wind turbines, stipulating that they must be sited at least 1,125 feet from the tip of the turbine’s nearest blade to the nearest adjacent property line.

short_description: S.B. 52 allows counties to veto specific projects and declare areas off-limits for large renewable energy projects.
long_description: Ohio Senate Bill 52 of 2021 grants counties the power to veto specific projects and to declare themselves categorically off-limits to large renewable energy projects, including wind farms of at least 5 MW and solar facilities of at least 50 MW. Counties can adopt binding resolutions to prohibit or limit such projects.

short_description: Adams County passed a resolution creating a restricted area for large solar farms.
long_description: In March 2024, the Adams County Commission passed a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 creating a restricted area for large solar farms in unincorporated areas of the county due to concerns about competing interests with farmland.

short_description: Allen County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind and solar projects in unincorporated areas.
long_description: On April 4, 2022, the Allen County Commission unanimously passed a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 declaring portions of the unincorporated areas of Allen County off-limits for economically significant wind farms and large solar facilities.

short_description: Auglaize County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind farms in unincorporated areas.
long_description: On April 26, 2022, the Auglaize County Commission unanimously passed a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 designating all unincorporated territories of the county as a restricted area for economically significant wind farms (at least 5 MW).

short_description: Brown County passed a resolution prohibiting large solar and wind projects in unincorporated areas.
long_description: In August 2022, the Brown County Board of Commissioners approved a resolution under S.B. 52 establishing all unincorporated areas of the county as a restricted area for large solar facilities and economically significant wind farms (at least 5 MW).

short_description: Butler County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind and solar projects in unincorporated areas.
long_description: On June 23, 2022, the Butler County Board of Commissioners passed a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 declaring all unincorporated areas of 12 townships off-limits for wind projects (at least 5 MW) and solar projects (at least 50 MW).

short_description: Clermont County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind and solar projects in seven townships.
long_description: In June 2023, the Clermont County Commissioners unanimously voted to prohibit large wind and solar projects in seven townships (Batavia, Jackson, Monroe, Stonelick, Tate, Washington, and Williamsburg) due to resident preferences. Two other townships (Goshen and Ohio) also voted to ban such projects but were too late for the meeting.

short_description: Columbiana County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind and solar projects in unincorporated areas.
long_description: On March 2, 2023, the Columbiana County Board of Commissioners approved a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 prohibiting large wind and solar farms in the unincorporated areas of four townships. By May 2023, additional bans were approved for seven more townships, with all eighteen townships ultimately banning such projects by October 18.

short_description: Crawford County passed a resolution prohibiting wind development for 10 years.
long_description: In May 2022, the Crawford County Board of Commissioners passed a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 creating a 10-year ban on wind development that effectively prevents construction of the proposed 300-MW Honey Creek Wind Project.

short_description: Erie County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind and solar projects in unincorporated areas.
long_description: In July 2023, Erie County voted to prohibit new industrial-scale wind and solar farms in all unincorporated land in the county, along with offshore wind farms in Lake Erie.

short_description: Fairfield County passed a resolution prohibiting large solar projects in certain areas.
long_description: In May 2024, the Fairfield County Commissioners adopted a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 prohibiting solar farms with a capacity of at least 50 MW within certain restricted areas due to balancing property owners' rights with their neighbors' concerns.

short_description: Fayette County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind and solar projects in unincorporated areas.
long_description: In January 2023, the Fayette County Board of Commissioners approved a resolution under S.B. 52 prohibiting large-scale wind and solar in all unincorporated areas of the county except for industrial areas.

short_description: Greene County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind and solar projects in certain areas.
long_description: In June 2023, the Greene County Board of Commissioners approved requests from five townships (Cedarville, Jefferson, Ross, Sugarcreek, and Xenia) to restrict large-scale solar and economically significant wind farms so that communities could maintain an agricultural outline. A similar request is being considered for a sixth township.

short_description: Hancock County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind and solar projects in unincorporated areas.
long_description: On April 19, 2022, the Hancock County Board of Commissioners adopted a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 prohibiting wind farms (at least 5 MW) and solar farms (at least 50 MW) from all unincorporated areas of the county except in Biglick Township.

short_description: Henry County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind and solar projects in unincorporated areas.
long_description: In December 2023, Henry County passed a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 declaring certain areas off-limits for large-scale wind and solar projects (at least 50 MW).

short_description: Knox County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind projects in unincorporated areas.
long_description: On August 11, 2022, the Knox County Board of Commissioners adopted a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 prohibiting large wind farms from unincorporated parts of the county but not solar farms.

short_description: Licking County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind and solar projects in certain townships.
long_description: In August 2024, Licking County Commissioners unanimously approved a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 prohibiting the development of large-scale solar and wind projects (at least 50 MW) in five townships: Hanover, Licking, St. Albans, Union, and Washington. Similar bans are already in effect for Liberty and Etna townships.

short_description: Logan County passed a resolution prohibiting large wind and solar projects in unincorporated areas.
long_description: On August 11, 2022, the Logan County Board of Commissioners passed a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 prohibiting wind farms (at least 5 MW) and solar farms (at least 50 MW) from all unincorporated areas of the county, with the exception of Miami Township.

short_description: State-level ban on wind and solar projects.
long_description: In 2019, Oklahoma passed a state law prohibiting the construction of new wind and solar energy facilities. This ban is currently in force.

short_description: Oklahoma Governor signed House Bill 2118 establishing setback requirements for wind turbines near military airspace.
long_description: In May 2019, Oklahoma Governor Kevin Sitt signed House Bill 2118 which established setback requirements for the construction of individual wind turbines near military airspace. The law requires developers to submit a 'Determination of No Hazard' from the Federal Aviation Administration and documentation showing that any adverse impacts to the Department of Defense have been resolved. Two weeks after the passage of the bill, NextEra Energy cancelled two proposed wind projects: Minco V and Crowder.

short_description: Owasso, Oklahoma passed a local ordinance requiring wind energy facilities to be set back 1.5 miles from public schools, hospitals, and airports.
long_description: Since August 21, 2015, the City of Owasso in Oklahoma has required that wind energy facilities be set back 1.5 miles from any public school, hospital, or airport.

short_description: Yukon, Oklahoma passed a local ordinance limiting the height of wind turbines abutting residential districts.
long_description: A 1995 ordinance in Yukon, Oklahoma limits the height of wind turbines abutting residential districts to 100 feet and limits rotor length to 36 feet in diameter.

short_description: Local community members organized to oppose the Cabin Creek Wind Farm project, a proposed 300-MW wind project.
long_description: Local community members have organized to oppose the Cabin Creek Wind Farm project, a proposed 300-MW wind project. A citizens group called ‘Craig County Concerned Citizens’ backed a zoning proposition on the ballot in November 2024 aimed at limiting wind farm expansions near homes. The opposition group sited concerns about health, safety, and property rights. The zoning proposition failed to win a majority of votes.

short_description: Community members organized protests and advocated for a moratorium on the Canadian River Wind Project, leading to its cancellation.
long_description: In response to the proposed 300-MW Canadian River wind farm, community members organized protests and advocated for a moratorium on wind farm development in the county. Local opponents expressed concerns over potential impacts on property values, water resources, and tourism. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation supported the efforts against the project, raising concerns about the lack of formal consultation with the tribes. In January 2025, the project developer announced its decision to terminate the development in response to local opposition.

short_description: Local community members organized to oppose the Cedar Run Wind Project, a proposed 97.5-MW wind farm.
long_description: Local community members have organized to oppose the Cedar Run Wind Project, a proposed 97.5-MW wind farm. The local opposition group has erected ‘no wind turbines’ signs throughout the county, launched a Facebook group that attracted more than 2,000 members, and erected a website expressing opposition to the project. The project faced a possible moratorium in the county, but the Lincoln County Commissioners ultimately decided not to vote on a moratorium.

short_description: The Osage Nation has contested the Osage Wind project on mineral rights grounds and brought legal action against Enel.
long_description: The Osage Nation has contested a wind farm developed by Enel in Osage County on the basis that the 84-turbine wind farm constitutes a trespass on Osage Nation mineral rights. Beginning in 2014, the federal government and Osage Mineral Council have brought suit against Osage Wind LLC. In 2016, a federal appellate judge held that the Osage Tribe had standing to seek damages for the operation of Osage Wind’s 8,400-acre wind farm and that Enel was unlawfully mining without a mineral permit by gathering and crushing rock to use for the base of its turbines. In January 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to consider an appeal from Osage Wind LLC. The parties were in court again in September 2023, where the Osage Mineral Council and federal government argued that Osage Wind was liable for continued trespass. In December 2023, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma held that Osage Wind was liable for continued trespass and ordered removal of the wind farm.

short_description: Local community members opposed the Skeleton Creek Solar Project and protested at a county board meeting.
long_description: On February 27, 2023, the Metropolitan Area Planning Commission denied an application by NextEra Energy Resources to use 5,277 acres of land for a solar and battery storage facility. Members of the public expressed concerns about glint and glare, as well as impacts to farm properties. NextEra has moved forward with the project, and in October 2023, roughly 90-100 people protested the project at a Garfield County Board of County Commissioners meeting.

project_or_policy_name: Department of Land Conservation and Development Solar Siting Rules
short_description: Oregon Department of Land Conservation and Development adopted regulations restricting solar facilities on farmland.
long_description: On May 23, 2019, the Oregon Department of Land Conservation and Development adopted regulations that restrict the construction of solar facilities on certain categories of farmland. The new rules do not allow solar facilities that use, occupy, or cover more than 12 acres of prime farmland or 20 acres of other farmland unless an exception applies.

short_description: Wind turbines must be set back from urban growth boundary, unincorporated community, and rural residences in Umatilla County.
long_description: Wind turbines must be set back 2 miles from the city urban growth boundary, 1 mile from land zoned as an unincorporated community, and 2 miles from a rural residence in Umatilla County.

short_description: A group challenged Clackamas County’s approval of a solar project on prime farmland.
long_description: In June 2018, a group called 1,000 Friends of Oregon filed an appeal challenging Clackamas County’s approval of a 73-acre solar project on prime farmland. The County had found that the project would not preclude commercial agriculture because it would house 100 honeybee colonies on site.

short_description: A group filed lawsuits to stop the transmission line project.
long_description: The 290-mile Boardman-to-Hemingway (B2H) transmission line, first proposed in 2007, would deliver up to 1,000 MW of renewable energy across eastern Oregon and southwestern Idaho. However, a group called the STOP B2H Coalition has filed at least two lawsuits to stop the project.

short_description: Public opposition led to the withdrawal of additional wind project proposals.
long_description: In 2007, Columbia Energy Partners proposed Echanis Wind Farm, a 104-MW wind farm on approximately 10,500 acres. The project met immediate opposition from the Oregon Natural Desert Association due to its proximity to the federally-protected Steens Mountain.

short_description: Neighbors appealed to the Oregon Land Use Board of Appeals after Clackamas County approved a solar project.
long_description: Mountain Meadow Solar, LLC applied to Clackamas County for permission to construct a 10-acre solar farm on a parcel then used for growing Christmas trees. Ager Clackamas County approved the project, five neighbors appealed to the Oregon Land Use Board of Appeals.

short_description: Local opposition to a large solar project includes letter-writing campaigns and advocacy for local control.
long_description: The proposed 199-MW Muddy Creek Energy Park solar energy generation facility would encompass 1,588 acres. The project is in the process of a two-year study mandated by the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife. However, this project has faced intense local opposition.

short_description: Local opposition led to the expansion of a wind project with solar and storage capacity.
long_description: In September 2017, Capital Power proposed a 350-MW wind project on approximately 45,000 acres in Umatilla County’s exclusive farm use zone. In November 2020, the project was expanded to include up to 300 MW of solar and storage capacity.

short_description: Local residents opposed a solar project due to dust and wildlife impacts.
long_description: Plans for the 400-MW Obsidian Solar Center in the high desert of Christmas Valley were met with opposition by local residents concerned about dust and impacts to local wildlife. The project was submitted for approval in 2018 but faced delays due to opposition.

short_description: An appeal challenged Jackson County’s approval of a solar project on prime farmland.
long_description: The group 1,000 Friends of Oregon filed an appeal challenging Jackson County’s approval of an 80-acre solar facility on prime farmland outside of Medford. The state’s Land Use Board of Appeals reversed the decision, siding with the opponents. In June 2018, the Oregon Court of Appeals upheld LUBA’s decision.

short_description: A lawsuit challenged the federal government’s approval of a wind farm on Steens Mountain.
long_description: In 2012, the Portland Audubon Society and Oregon Natural Desert Association filed a lawsuit in federal court to challenge the federal government’s approval of a wind farm on Steens Mountain. The lawsuit cited potential impacts to golden eagles, sage grouse, and bighorn sheep.

short_description: State-level prohibitions on wind and solar projects were enacted in 2019-2020.
long_description: Pennsylvania has implemented state-level prohibitions on both wind and solar energy projects, which have been adopted between 2019 and 2020. These restrictions are currently in force.

short_description: Pennsylvania Game Commission approved a wind energy moratorium on over 1.5 million acres of game lands in April 2018.
long_description: In April 2018, the Pennsylvania Game Commission unanimously approved a wind energy moratorium across over 1.5 million acres of game lands in the state. The Commission stated that it recognizes the value in renewable energy systems but that the construction and operation of wind energy would threaten the habitat stability of game and other species in the area.

project_or_policy_name: Solar Development Ban on Agricultural Land
short_description: North Beaver Township passed an ordinance in 2021 prohibiting solar development on agricultural land.
long_description: In 2021, North Beaver Township passed an ordinance that prohibits solar development on agricultural land. The decision was partially in response to protests of Vesper Energy’s proposed Firefly Solar project and has hindered the project's development.

short_description: Ralpho Township adopted a solar ordinance in November 2022, allowing major solar energy systems as a special exception in agricultural and forestry land but not residential areas.
long_description: In November 2022, Ralpho Township adopted a solar ordinance that allows major solar energy systems as a special exception in land zoned for agriculture and forestry, but not in residential areas. In December 2022, the owner of an amusement park who intended to build a 15-acre solar array in a residential district filed a lawsuit challenging the ordinance.

short_description: Smith Township amended its solar ordinance in September 2024, increasing setbacks and requiring additional reports.
long_description: In July 2024, the Smith Township Planning Commission began discussions to amend its solar ordinance. On September 4, 2024, the Commission held a special meeting to discuss the proposed revisions. On September 18, 2024, the Commission voted unanimously to submit the proposed amendments to the Board of Supervisors for approval. On November 12, 2024, the Board unanimously voted to adopt the new solar ordinance 2024-5.

short_description: AtlanDc Wind proposed a wind turbine project in Carbon County but faced legal challenges.
long_description: In 2016, AtlanDc Wind submitted a proposal to construct 37 wind turbines in Penn Forest Township on lands owned by the Bethlehem Municipal Authority. The 2016 proposal was “deemed approved” when Penn Forest Township defaulted on deadline during the review process. Township residents filed a lawsuit challenging the deemed approval, but the approval was upheld in December 2017 by a Carbon County judge. In 2018, with the first application still pending, AtlanDc Wind submitted a modified application seeking permission for only 28 turbines located farther from homes.

short_description: Residents protested a large solar project in Mount Joy Township, leading to legal challenges.
long_description: During a series of 21 public hearings between January 2020 and March 2021, residents protested a 75-MW solar energy project proposed by Brookfield Solar I LLC that would span 1,000 acres across 26 different parcels of land in Mount Joy Township. At one hearing in August 2020, protestors argued that the town supervisor should be fired because he owns a solar lease. In June 2021, Mount Joy Township supervisors rejected the developer’s request for a conditional use permit to build a 391-acre stretch of the project along a major highway. On September 2, 2022, the Court of Common Pleas of Adams County, Pennsylvania upheld the denial of the permit, finding that the developer failed to provide sufficient analysis of adverse impacts on surrounding property owners.

short_description: Project neighbors opposed the Brookview Solar 1 project in Lancaster County.
long_description: In November 2023, the Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court affirmed the denial of a permit for the Brookview Solar 1 project in Mt. Joy Township. Project neighbors had opposed the development, collecting 950 signatures for a petition against the project.

short_description: A pumped storage project faced opposition from local groups and environmentalists.
long_description: York Energy Storage LLC plans to construct a 1.8-mile-long dam and flood 580 acres to create a hydroelectric facility designed to feed power into the regional grid. The project is named the Cuffs Run Pumped Storage Project and will have an estimated 1,000-acre footprint. In July 2023, a coalition of 17 nonprofits and local governments, along with Republican State Senator KrisDn Phillips-Hill of York, signed a letter urging federal regulators to reject the preliminary permit application for the project. The letter states that the “proposed project would destroy preserved farms, a regional scenic trail, and forested lands much needed to help protect the ecological health of this landscape and waterway.” In September 2023, FERC rejected the preliminary permit application due to deficiencies in the application; the application was refiled and accepted in February 2024.

short_description: The Dover Solar I Project faced significant local opposition but was ultimately approved.
long_description: Enel Green Power’s plans to construct a 600-acre solar project in Dover Township encountered local opposition. One group called Keep Dover BeauDful started a website to organize opposition against the project. The project was ultimately approved in 2022 after eight meetings.

short_description: The Electric City Solar Initiative faced local opposition and zoning approval denial.
long_description: In February 2023, the Scranton Zoning Board denied zoning approval to ECA Solar for the construction of a solar farm on West Mountain. The Massachusetts-based company sought to re-zone 73 acres of land to install over 12,000 solar panels. Some residents had complained that the project would be visually disruptive and would lead to flooding from stormwater runoff.

short_description: Vesper Energy's Firefly Solar project faced significant local opposition and was ultimately prohibited on agricultural land.
long_description: Vesper Energy’s proposal to construct the 200-MW Firefly Solar project on prime farmland in North Beaver Township led to significant pushback, and the township ultimately prohibited solar development on agricultural land in 2021. Vesper continued to attempt to develop the project in Lawrence County.

short_description: A solar farm project in Greenfield Township faced local opposition and required additional environmental reports.
long_description: New Leaf Energy’s plans to construct a solar project on 23 acres of land zoned for suburban-residential development in Greenfield Township have encountered local opposition. At a hearing in January 2023, residents expressed concerns about runoff and impacts to the environment, property values, and the town's rural character.

short_description: Rhode Island enacted a solar siting bill that prohibits developing solar farms in core forests.
long_description: In 2023, Rhode Island enacted a solar siting bill that increases the annual statewide cap on new Renewable Energy Growth developments from 40 MW to 300 MW per year but prohibits participating developers from developing solar farms in 'core forests'. Core forests are defined as unfragmented forest blocks of single or multiple parcels totaling at least 250 acres and at least 25 yards from mapped roads. Exceptions could be allowed for projects already underway or on preferred sites within core forests.

short_description: Warwick, Rhode Island adopted a 6-month moratorium on ground-mounted solar projects and later prohibited large-scale solar energy projects.
long_description: In November 2021, the City of Warwick, Rhode Island adopted a 6-month moratorium on ground-mounted solar projects. In March 2022, the city adopted a new ordinance that prohibits large-scale solar energy projects and limits height to 10 feet.

short_description: Cranston, Rhode Island adopted new zoning rules allowing solar farms only in two industrial districts.
long_description: In February 2020, the City of Cranston adopted new zoning rules that allow solar farms only in the two industrial districts.

short_description: Foster, Rhode Island banned wind turbines in residential areas but requires town council approval.
long_description: In April 2021, the Foster Planning Board voted 5-1 to ban wind turbines from the residential areas of their town. Two of the board members had lived close to wind turbines and expressed that their families had been negatively impacted by the sound and shadow flicker. In order to go into effect, however, the amendment would require the Town Council’s final approval.

short_description: North Kingstown, Rhode Island placed a moratorium on wind turbines and later banned them.
long_description: In January 2011, the Town of North Kingstown placed a 6-month moratorium, which was extended by 90 days in June 2011. In November 2011, the Town Council voted to prohibit all wind turbines in the town pending the issuance of a state report anticipated in early 2012. The moratorium was motivated by opposition to a proposal to construct two wind turbines in the town. However, those two turbines were not subject to the moratorium. As of March 2023, wind energy systems are prohibited in the town, not including any approved prior to November 21, 2011.

project_or_policy_name: 6-month moratorium on solar farms outside industrial areas
short_description: Calhoun County adopted a 6-month moratorium on solar farms outside industrial areas in unincorporated areas.
long_description: In March 2023, the Calhoun County Council adopted a 6-month moratorium on the development of solar farms outside of industrial areas in unincorporated areas of the county. The moratorium did not apply to previously approved solar projects.

project_or_policy_name: 500-foot setbacks from town and subdivision boundaries
short_description: Calhoun County approved a solar ordinance establishing 500-foot setbacks from town and subdivision boundaries.
long_description: In October 2023, the county approved a solar ordinance that established 500-foot setbacks from town and subdivision boundaries.

short_description: Southern Current proposed a 138-MW, 1,500-acre solar project near Gallivants Ferry but faced opposition and never built.
long_description: During meetings in 2020, members of the County Council raised concerns about leaching of cadmium telluride, questioning what would happen if the solar panels were damaged in a hurricane. County Council members also raised concerns about decommissioning and whether landfills would accept solar panels. Although the developer agreed not to use solar panels that include cadmium telluride, the project was never built.

short_description: Runnymede LLC proposed a 2-MW solar project but faced opposition and permit challenges.
long_description: On April 29, 2022, Runnymede LLC submitted an application to build a 2-MW solar system on 44 acres of land zoned for heavy industrial use in the Runnymede subdivision of Sumner City. On May 26, 2022, the local zoning authorities issued a permit. However, on June 27, 2022, the owners of property within the Runnymede subdivision filed an appeal challenging the project. At a meeting on August 10, the Zoning Board of Appeals upheld the permit with three additional conditions, including landscaping requirements.

project_or_policy_name: Hughes County Wind Energy Development Moratorium
short_description: Hughes County approved a 6-month moratorium on wind energy development to review setback requirements.
long_description: In May 2017, the Hughes County Commission in South Dakota approved a 6-month moratorium on wind energy development. The moratorium was intended to allow for a review of setback requirements in the local zoning ordinance. One commissioner expressed concerns about competing land uses between wind and cattle grazing.

short_description: Letcher Township increased setbacks for wind turbines to 1 mile from residences of non-participating landowners and 1,500 feet from property lines.
long_description: In 2016, the Letcher Township Board of Supervisors in Sanborn County passed an ordinance increasing setbacks for wind turbines. The new setback requirements were set to 1 mile from residences of non-participating landowners and 1,500 feet from property lines.

short_description: Lincoln County increased the minimum setback from habitable residences to 0.5 miles for wind turbines.
long_description: In 2017, Lincoln County in South Dakota enacted new zoning laws that increased the minimum setback from habitable residences to 0.5 miles (2,640 feet) for wind turbines. This change was motivated by and led to the cancellation of a proposed 1,000-MW project by Dakota Power Community Wind.

project_or_policy_name: Countywide Moratorium on Utility-Scale Alternative Energy Systems
short_description: Pennington County adopted a countywide moratorium on utility-scale alternative energy systems for one year.
long_description: On November 19, 2024, the Pennington County Board of Commissioners in South Dakota adopted a countywide moratorium on utility-scale alternative energy systems, including both solar and wind energy systems. The moratorium is set to expire on November 18, 2025.

short_description: Walworth County increased setback requirements for wind turbines to 2 miles from existing residences and businesses.
long_description: In May 2017, Walworth County in South Dakota adopted an ordinance requiring that wind turbines be set back 2 miles from existing residences, businesses, and churches. In November 2023, the county increased setback requirements for solar farms to 1 mile from residences and 1,000 feet from property lines.

short_description: Geronimo Energy proposed a 400-MW wind farm, but the final project was reduced to 200 MW due to setbacks.
long_description: In 2017, Geronimo Energy proposed a 400-MW wind farm in Clark County. Public hearings on the project featured significant opposition from local residents. The Clark County Commission approved the project but required that turbines be set back 3,960 feet (0.75 miles) from residences, far more than the 1,000 feet required by the county zoning ordinance. Geronimo Energy challenged the setback requirements in court, but the court ruled in favor of the commission. South Dakota’s Public Utilities Commission granted a construction permit in June 2018. The final project, completed in 2019, was 200 MW, half the size originally proposed.

short_description: The 132-turbine Crowned Ridge Wind project was appealed to the South Dakota Supreme Court.
long_description: The Public Utility Commission’s permit for the 132-turbine Crowned Ridge Wind project was appealed by opponents to the South Dakota Supreme Court, which upheld it in 2022. One of the landowners who brought the appeal later filed a suit about the noise level from the operating wind farm. In October 2023, that complaint was dismissed after the plaintiff failed to attend a hearing.

short_description: Local residents organized an opposition group to advocate for stricter setbacks. The project was cancelled in 2017.
long_description: In 2014, the Dakota Power Community Wind proposed a 1,000-MW wind farm in rural Lincoln County with up to 500 turbines. Local residents organized an opposition group, We-Care SD, to advocate for stricter setbacks. The Lincoln County Board of Commissioners increased the setback requirement from 0.25 miles to 0.5 miles from habitable dwellings. Voters upheld the setbacks in a July 2017 referendum. In November 2017, the developer relinquished 122 easements it had secured for the project, signaling an intent to cancel the project.

short_description: Davison County Commissioners rejected a conditional use permit application for the construction of 9 wind turbines.
long_description: In April 2018, the Davison County Commissioners in South Dakota unanimously voted to reject a conditional use permit application for the construction of 9 wind turbines in Beulah Township. It marked the second time in three years that the Commission had rejected a wind energy project. Several Commissioners expressed concern about potential impacts on solar developments.

project_or_policy_name: Juhl Energy’s Davison County Wind Project
short_description: Juhl Energy’s 9-to-11-turbine wind farm project was denied due to neighbors' concerns about property value impacts and quality of life.
long_description: In February 2016, the Davison County Commission in South Dakota denied a permit for a 9-to-11-turbine wind farm proposed by Juhl Energy. The project faced intense opposition from neighbors due to concerns about property value impacts and quality of life.

short_description: Letcher Township increased setbacks to 1 mile from dwellings of non-participating homeowners and 1,500 feet from property lines.
long_description: In 2016, residents of Letcher Township in Sanborn County pre-emptively mobilized to block Juhl Energy from developing a wind project. Although Juhl Energy had not yet submitted an application, residents were concerned that the company would look to Letcher Township after nearby Davison County rejected its applicaion for a 9-to-11-turbine wind farm. Out of 77 registered voters in Letcher Township, 50 signed a petition opposing the project. In response to the petition, the Board of Supervisors voted to increase setbacks to 1 mile from dwellings of non-participating homeowners and 1,500 feet from property lines, making the project impossible to site.

project_or_policy_name: National Grid Renewables McCook County Solar Farm
short_description: National Grid Renewables withdrew an application for a solar farm in McCook County due to local opposition, then resubmitted.
long_description: In February 2023, National Grid Renewables withdrew an application for a solar farm in McCook County amidst significant local opposition. The company then filed a second application. In November 2023, the McCook County Commission delayed a vote on the project after two hours of public testimony in a meeting with over fifty residents. The Commission stated that it needed to further consider impacts on neighborhood characteristics, the environment, and adjacent projects.

short_description: Walworth County residents opposed the Oahe Solar project, citing concerns about tourism, water, and fire risk.
long_description: Walworth County residents have opposed plans for the 3,200-acre Oahe Solar project, citing concerns about impacts to tourism, water, and fire risk. Residents stated that they are not anti-solar but seek greater protections in the planning process. In response to local concerns, in November 2023, the county increased setback requirements for solar farms to 1 mile from residences and 1,000 feet from property lines.

short_description: Tennessee passed a ban on new utility-scale solar and wind projects in 2019.
long_description: In 2019, Tennessee enacted legislation that prohibits the construction of new utility-scale solar and wind energy facilities. This ban is effective statewide and applies to both public and private utilities.

short_description: Tennessee passed HB 1731 of 2018, setting minimum requirements for wind facilities and imposing a moratorium on certain projects.
long_description: HB 1731 of 2018 sets minimum setback requirements for wind facilities in Tennessee. Local legislation must include a minimum setback requirement of 3.5 times the turbine height from non-participating property lines, with exceptions for landowner waivers and specific elevation restrictions on turbines.

short_description: Tennessee passed HB 1021/SB 1336, imposing a one-year moratorium on wind energy facility construction.
long_description: HB 1021/SB 1336 imposed a one-year moratorium on the construction of new wind energy facilities in Tennessee. The moratorium included an exemption for counties and municipalities that had adopted regulations by July 1, 2017, and established a study committee to evaluate siting issues.

short_description: Franklin County adopted a resolution indefinitely prohibiting commercial renewable-energy facilities.
long_description: In April 2022, the Franklin County Commission adopted a resolution indefinitely prohibiting commercial renewable-energy facilities within the county.

short_description: Greene County approved a 6-month moratorium on new commercial farms.
long_description: In August 2022, the Greene County Commission approved a 6-month moratorium on new commercial farms within the county.

project_or_policy_name: 180-day moratorium on commercial solar farm developments
short_description: Shelby County approved an 180-day moratorium on commercial solar farm developments in the Conservation Agricultural zoning district.
long_description: In September 2023, the Shelby County Commission approved a 180-day moratorium on new commercial solar farm developments within the Conservation Agricultural zoning district of unincorporated Shelby County.

short_description: Shelby County Board of Commissioners denied the Graceland Solar Project, following opposition from residents and a Change.org petition.
long_description: The Shelby County Board of Commissioners denied the 150-MW Graceland Solar Project in February 2024. The project faced vocal opposition from local residents during previous meetings with the Division of Planning and Development. A Change.org petition also opposed the project, asking Shelby County to deny it.

short_description: Texas state government has enacted bans on wind and solar projects in certain areas.
long_description: The Texas state government has implemented a series of bans on the development of wind and solar energy projects in specific regions, citing environmental concerns and land use issues. These restrictions have been adopted over several years from 2019 to 2023, with ongoing legal challenges.

short_description: City of Balch Springs prohibits wind energy systems larger than 20 kW and sets height limits.
long_description: The city code prohibits wind energy systems larger than 20 kW and sets a height limit of 70 feet. Small wind energy systems are allowed provided they do not exceed the maximum building height plus 5 feet, with noise limited to 35 dBa at night.

short_description: City of Benbrook prohibits utility-scale wind projects and limits solar to accessory use.
long_description: The municipal code of ordinances prohibits utility-scale wind projects. Small wind energy systems are allowed provided they do not exceed the maximum building height plus 5 feet, with noise limited to 35 dBa at night. Likewise, solar is only allowed as an accessory use.

short_description: City of Brownsville limits wind turbine height and solar installation areas.
long_description: The City of Brownsville limits the height limit of wind turbines to 70 feet in residential zones and 120 feet in all other areas. The ordinance limits ground-mounted solar installations to side or rear yard, with large-scale systems not allowed in Dwelling or Dwelling/Retail use districts.

short_description: City of Burleson sets height and setback limits for wind turbines.
long_description: The City of Burleson specifies that turbines be no more than 120 feet tall on any parcel of 5 or more acres, and 60 feet tall on any parcel of less than 5 acres. Turbines must be set back at least 1,000 feet from all interstate and state rights-of-way, with noise limits of 40 dB at adjacent residential property lines.

short_description: City of Denison allows wind turbines only as accessory use for on-site power consumption.
long_description: The city allows wind turbines only as an accessory use for on-site power consumption and creates a setback of 2 times the tower height from all property lines.

short_description: City of Garland limits wind turbine height and requires rear yard placement.
long_description: An ordinance adopted May 2015 provides that wind turbines may only exist as a secondary use, must be located in the rear yard of any lot, and must be limited to 40 feet in height.

short_description: City of Grand Prairie allows small wind energy systems with a nameplate capacity of 100 kW or less.
long_description: The only wind energy systems allowed in the City of Grand Prairie are small wind energy systems with a nameplate capacity of 100 kW or less whose primary purpose is on-site power use.

short_description: City of Kingsville allows commercial wind turbines only in industrial districts.
long_description: Enacted in April 2014, this ordinance allows commercial wind turbines only in the city’s industrial districts, where turbine height is limited to 100 feet. In all other districts, wind energy systems are only allowed as an accessory use, and turbine height is limited to either 45 feet or 10 feet above building height, whichever is less.

short_description: City of McKinney allows wind turbines only as accessory use for on-site power generation.
long_description: The city’s zoning regulations allow wind turbines only as an accessory use for onsite generation and prohibits even small turbines from residential districts.

short_description: City of Midlothian allows wind turbines only for on-site power generation.
long_description: A local ordinance in the City of Midlothian, last updated in 2019, allows wind turbines only for on-site power generation. It allows only one wind turbine per lot, unless the lot is 3 acres or larger, in which case it allows two turbines. Height is limited to 80 feet unless authorized by special use permit.

short_description: City of Nolanville prohibits leasing land or establishing wind energy units within city limits.
long_description: An ordinance adopted in May 2012 provides that the leasing of land or establishment of wind energy units on land for the commercial sale of wind energy is prohibited within the City limits.

short_description: City of Ovilla limits noise from wind turbines.
long_description: The city zoning ordinance provides that noise from wind turbines shall not exceed 40 dBA during the day or 30 dBA at night at the most offending property line.

short_description: City of Waller allows small wind energy systems in four corridors.
long_description: The City of Waller allows small wind energy systems but only as an accessory use on property owned by the owner of the wind energy system. Small wind energy systems are allowed only in four established corridors in the city, and turbines are limited to 45 feet in height at the center of the swath.

short_description: City of Weatherford limits wind turbine max blade height.
long_description: The city allows wind turbines only as an accessory use and limits turbine max blade diameter height to 66 feet.

short_description: Bluegrove Wind Project was canceled after opposition from local residents and politicians.
long_description: John Greer, a Dallas oil investor with a family ranch in Clay County, spearheaded a multiyear fight against the proposed 100-MW Bluegrove wind project. Greer helped co-found Clay County Against Wind Farms, which held informational sessions against wind energy in Henrietta, Texas. In June 2018, under pressure from residents and politicians, Innergex Renewable Energy Inc. formally canceled the project.

short_description: Byers Wind Project was canceled after opposition from local residents and politicians.
long_description: John Greer, a Dallas oil investor with a family ranch in Clay County, spearheaded a multiyear fight against the proposed utility-scale Byers wind project. Greer helped co-found Clay County Against Wind Farms, which held informational sessions against wind energy in Henrietta, Texas. In June 2018, under pressure from residents and politicians, Innergex Renewable Energy Inc. formally canceled the project.

short_description: Horse Hollow Wind Energy Center faced legal challenges over aesthetics and nuisance claims.
long_description: POWTL, a group of local residents, sued the wind farm for drastically disrupting the local scenery. The court ruled that no law in Texas regulates aesthetics, prompting the plaintiffs to amend the complaint to assert public and private nuisance claims and seek injunctive relief. In December 2006, a trial jury found against the plaintiffs. The case was dismissed, and the plaintiffs appealed. In August 2008, the Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment of the trial court on all respects except for the allocation of costs and remanded for further determination.

short_description: Mustang Wind Project faced opposition from local residents and an organized group.
long_description: Apex Clean Energy proposed a 250-MW wind farm within a 50,000-acre area north of Schulenburg. The development would include between 40 to 80 turbines, some up to 600 feet tall. Local opponents organized a Facebook page called “Fayette County Texas - Stop The Wind Turbines” and an opposition group called “FayCoSaysNo.” The groups were active at town hall meetings and recruited hundreds of residents to join in opposition.

short_description: Kane County adopted an ordinance in 2013 requiring utility-scale solar facilities to be set back at least 0.5 miles from the nearest inhabitable structure.
long_description: An ordinance was adopted in Kane County, Utah, on August 27, 2013, mandating that utility-scale solar power facilities must maintain a setback of at least 0.5 miles from any inhabited structures.

short_description: Vermont enacted a ban on new wind projects in 2019.
long_description: In 2019, Vermont passed legislation prohibiting the construction of new utility-scale wind energy facilities. This ban was implemented to address local concerns and opposition from residents and environmental groups regarding visual impacts and noise pollution.

short_description: Northeast Vermont Development Association unanimously approved a resolution against industrial-scale wind energy development.
long_description: In January 2015, the Northeastern Vermont Development Association (NVDA) — one of eleven Vermont regional planning commissions — unanimously approved a resolution against the development of all industrial wind energy systems. This position was reaffirmed in NVDA’s June 2023 memorandum readopting their 2018 Energy Plan.

project_or_policy_name: Apple Hill Solar and Willow Road Solar (f/k/a Chelsea Solar)
adopted_or_event_date_text: January 2018, May 2020, June 2019, January 2023, June 2023, July 2023, October 2023, December 2023
short_description: Allco Renewable Energy's Apple Hill and Willow Road solar projects have faced opposition from neighbors for over a decade, with legal challenges ongoing.
long_description: Allco Renewable Energy’s plans for the 2-MW Apple Hill project and 2-MW Willow Road project in Bennington, Vermont have faced opposition from neighbors. The state Public Utility Commission initially approved the Apple Hill project in 2018 but reversed its decision on remand in May 2020. In June 2019, the PUC denied a certificate of public good for the Willow Road project due to it being part of a larger solar plant. Legal challenges and opposition continued through multiple decisions and lawsuits.

short_description: Developer requested permission to change the site of a proposed solar project due to significant opposition from neighbors.
long_description: On March 30, 2018, the developer of a proposed 2.2-MW solar project near downtown Brandon wrote a letter to the Vermont Public Utility Commission requesting permission to change the site of the project because of ‘significant opposition to the project from neighboring property owners and residents due to aesthetic concerns.’

short_description: AllEarth Renewables proposed a single wind turbine project but faced significant delays and opposition, ultimately dropping the plans.
long_description: In July 2016, AllEarth Renewables proposed a single 2.2-MW wind turbine on a 450-acre dairy farm in the Town of Holland after winning a state contract. The project was stymied by significant delays at the Public Utility Commission and Governor Phil Scott’s stringent decibel limits for wind turbines. In January 2020, the developer announced that it was dropping plans for the project due to opposition.

short_description: Developer abandoned plans for a single-turbine wind project amidst local opposition.
long_description: In 2022, the developer of a proposed single-turbine, 1.5-MW wind project in Castleton, Vermont and surrounding towns abandoned plans amid local opposition. The failure followed an unsuccessful 2012 proposal for 20 turbines along the ridgeline at Grandpa’s Knob that was unanimously opposed by the Castleton Select Board.

short_description: Vermont Public Utility Commission rejected an application for a wind project due to incomplete information and local opposition.
long_description: In July 2017, the Vermont Public Utility Commission rejected an application for a certificate of public good for the Kidder Hill Wind project. The Commission stated that the application was incomplete and missing crucial information. In August of the same year, the Commission denied a motion for reconsideration. A local opponent stated: ‘The basic opposition comes from a place of community.’

short_description: Energize Vermont and several individuals challenged the issuance of a permit for a wind project, but the Supreme Court upheld it.
long_description: Several individuals joined with Energize Vermont in filing a lawsuit to challenge the issuance of a permit related to stormwater management at the 21-turbine Kingdom Community Wind Project. In 2013, the Vermont Supreme Court found ‘no clear and convincing error’ and affirmed the issuance of the permit.

short_description: Vermont Public Utility Commission denied a certificate for a solar project in Manchester due to aesthetic concerns.
long_description: In September 2021, the Vermont Public Utility Commission denied a certificate to a 500-kilowatt project in Manchester, Vermont, proposed by Manchester-based MHG Solar. The Commission cited aesthetic concerns and noted that it had received ‘many public comments in opposition to the project,’ primarily focused on aesthetic impacts and flooding concerns.

short_description: Amended zoning ordinance prohibits large wind projects in agricultural districts and requires special use permits for solar projects.
long_description: In January 2017, Accomack County amended its zoning ordinance to prohibit large wind projects in agricultural districts and to require large solar projects in agricultural districts to receive special use permits from the board of zoning appeals.

short_description: Revised zoning ordinance caps utility-scale solar projects to 50 acres and prohibits new projects within 1 mile of existing ones.
long_description: In March 2024, the Amherst County Board of Supervisors unanimously passed a revised zoning ordinance that establishes a cap of 50 acres under panel for utility-scale solar facilities. It also prohibits the siting of new solar projects within 1 mile of existing solar projects.

short_description: Comprehensive plan update limits solar projects to 200 acres in urban areas and prohibits new projects within 2 miles of existing ones.
long_description: In July 2021, the Augusta County Board of Supervisors updated the Utilities section of the County’s Comprehensive Plan to establish policies that would limit the size of industrial solar facilities. The update provided that solar farms are strongly discouraged from using more than 200 acres of land and that they should not be built in Urban Service and Community Development areas. In December 2023, Augusta County prohibited new solar projects in urban service and community development areas; at the same time, Augusta mandated that new solar projects must be located at least 2 miles from existing solar projects.

short_description: Solar ordinance limits cumulative solar development to 8,600 acres.
long_description: Brunswick County’s zoning ordinance limits the cumulative acreage of solar development in the county to 8,600 acres. In March 2023, the Brunswick County Board of Supervisors amended the solar ordinance to clarify that this acreage refers to the land under PV panel coverage, not the total acreage of the solar farm parcels.

short_description: Solar ordinance limits cumulative solar development to 1,600 MW or 7,500 acres.
long_description: In December 2023, Buckingham County adopted a solar ordinance that limits cumulative solar development to 1,600 MW or 7,500 acres.

short_description: Moratorium on solar project applications until January 1, 2024 or until zoning recommendations are made.
long_description: On August 8, 2022, the CharloWe County Board of Supervisors adopted a moratorium on applicaDons for solar projects through January 1, 2024, or unDl the CharloWe County Planning Commission makes a recommendaDon on zoning for solar projects, whichever happens first. In April 2023, CharloWe County liged the moratorium.

short_description: Zoning ordinance requires solar facilities to be located within 1 mile of two specified electrical substations.
long_description: As of January 2024, Clarke County’s zoning ordinance requires that all solar energy facilities, except for those delivering behind-the-meter power, be located within 1 mile of two specified electrical substations in the county. At the time of adoption, one solar project had already been built adjacent to one of the substations, and another project had already been proposed adjacent to the other substation.

policy_mechanism: cap on acreage, cap on project size
short_description: Solar ordinance limits utility-scale solar to 2,400 acres and individual projects to 300 acres.
long_description: On February 7, 2023, the Culpeper County Board of Supervisors voted to limit the size of future solar energy projects to 300 acres per project and to limit the total acreage for utility-scale solar to 2,400 acres.

short_description: Solar ordinance restricts new projects based on existing project area.
long_description: Fauquier County’s solar ordinance, passed in October 2020, mandates that no more than 8% of the land in a 2.5-mile radius of the project area of any existing utility-scale solar project can be approved for use as the project area for a new utility-scale solar project.

short_description: Solar ordinance limits above-ground solar projects to 1,500 acres and requires a setback of 300 feet from off-site residential structures.
long_description: On February 21, 2023, the Franklin County Board of Supervisors adopted an ordinance that imposed a 1,500-acre cap on above-ground solar projects countywide and a 300-foot setback from any off-site residenDal structures.

project_or_policy_name: Comprehensive Plan and Zoning Ordinance Amendments
project_area_acres: 500 acres, 1 mile from town/city boundaries, 2 miles from existing projects, 2 miles from transmission line corridors
short_description: Amendments regulate utility-scale solar and wind projects with a cap of 500 acres and specific setbacks.
long_description: In June 2024 the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously in favor of amendments to the county’s Comprehensive Plan and Zoning Ordinance to regulate renewable energy facilities. The amendments define utility-scale solar projects as those with a capacity of 1 MW or greater and limit the total size of any such projects to 500 acres. The amendments further require that such projects be set back at least 1 mile from any town or city boundary and at least 2 miles from any existing solar project. Further, any solar projects interconnecting to the grid must be located within 2 miles of transmission line corridors.

policy_mechanism: cap on acreage, cap on project size
short_description: Solar ordinance requires a minimum of 100 acres and caps cumulative acreage at 7,600 acres.
long_description: In March 2022, Greensville County passed an ordinance requiring all solar facilities to be a minimum of 100 acres and capping the cumulative acreage of solar farms in the county to 7,600 acres.

project_area_acres: 2% of prime farm soils, 72% already set aside
short_description: Zoning amendment limits solar development to 2% of prime farm soils and moratorium on new projects.
long_description: In May 2023, Isle of Wight County adopted an ordinance that limits solar farm acreage to 2% of prime farm soils, amounting to a maximum of 2,446 acres; as of 2017, 72% of that land was already set aside for approved solar farms.

short_description: Board of Supervisors establishes indefinite pause on new solar projects.
long_description: After rejecting an application by Pivot Energy to construct a solar farm in March 2023, the James City Board of Supervisors established an indefinite pause on new solar projects as it considered updates to its solar farm regulations.

policy_mechanism: cap on acreage, cap on project size
short_description: Solar ordinance limits cumulative solar development to 9,800 acres or 3% of county land.
long_description: As of its August 2022 solar ordinance, Louisa County limits solar farms to a maximum cumulative acreage of 9,800 acres or 3% of county land.

short_description: Grant County adopted a moratorium on new commercial or industrial wind or solar projects.
long_description: On August 3, 2021, the Grant County Board of County Commissioners adopted a moratorium on new commercial or industrial wind or solar projects. The moratorium was extended by 90 days in January 25, 2022.

short_description: Kittitas County Commissioners established a temporary moratorium on major solar energy projects.
long_description: In early 2017, the Kittitas County Commissioners established a temporary moratorium on applications for major solar energy projects. The moratorium was extended by another six months in July of 2017 and created a Citizen Advisory Committee to gather information. The moratorium was rescinded in October 2018 with the adoption of a new ordinance.

short_description: Klickitat County adopted a 6-month moratorium on solar projects greater than 1 acre.
long_description: On January 10, 2023, the Klickitat County Commissioners adopted a 6-month moratorium on solar projects greater than 1 acre in the Goldendale and Centerville valleys. An ordinance adopted August 17, 2010, requires wind turbines to be set back 1,600 feet from existing residential structures and solar panels by 'a minimum of five hundred [500] to one thousand five hundred [1,500] feet' depending on aesthetic impacts, geography, and project size.

short_description: Yakima County adopted a temporary moratorium on mid- and large-scale solar projects.
long_description: On July 26, 2022, Yakima County adopted a temporary moratorium on mid- and large-scale solar projects. The moratorium was extended for another 6 months on February 28, 2023, and again until February 15, 2024.

short_description: The Badger Mountain Solar Project is a 200-MW solar project proposed by Aurora Solar, LLC. Indigenous people have objected to the planned construction.
long_description: The Badger Mountain Solar Project is a 200-MW solar project proposed by Aurora Solar, LLC, a subsidiary of Avangrid Renewables, LLC. Wenatchi-P’squosa people indigenous to the area have objected to the planned construction, citing concerns that the project threatens cultural resources including foodways and sacred sites on the mountain. In May 2023, the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation formally registered their opposition to the project.

short_description: The Carriger Solar Project is a proposed 160-MW solar project. Citizens Educated About Solar Energy (CEASE) opposed the project, and the Klickitat County Commission adopted a moratorium.
long_description: The proposed 160-MW Carriger Solar Project drew opposition from a group called Citizens Educated About Solar Energy (CEASE). In August 2021, the founder of CEASE was ejected from a public meeting about the project for causing a disruption. On January 10, 2023, the Klickitat County Commission adopted a 6-month moratorium on solar projects in the area where the project has been proposed.

short_description: The Columbia Solar Project is a proposed 25-MW solar project. Neighbors opposed the project, and it was approved after a moratorium.
long_description: Tuusso Energy applied to the State Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC) for permission to construct a 25-MW, 200-acre solar project across five parcels of private property. Neighbors of the site started an organization, Save Our Farms, to advocate against the project. In early 2017, the Kittitas County Commission enacted a temporary moratorium that prohibited major solar projects.

short_description: The Goldendale Energy Storage Project is a proposed pumped storage project. The Yakama Nation opposes the project due to cultural concerns.
long_description: The Yakama Nation has been fighting the proposed Goldendale Energy Storage Project on its ancestral land for five years due to concerns that the pumped storage project could destroy tribal cultural property. The project is planned to be constructed on a 680-acre site with the capacity to generate 1,200-MW of energy.

short_description: Tenaska proposed a 200-MW battery energy storage system in Skagit County. Local residents raised concerns about fire and environmental hazards.
long_description: In June 2024, Tenaska submitted a proposal for a 200-MW battery energy storage system to the Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC) rather than seeking approval from Skagit County. The project is proposed to be located on approximately 16 acres zoned for agriculture in the outskirts of Sedro-Woolley. At a public hearing held in August 2024, local residents raised concerns of fire and environmental hazards.

short_description: West Virginia passed a ban on new wind energy projects in 2019-2020.
long_description: In 2019-2020, West Virginia enacted a state law prohibiting the construction of new utility-scale wind energy projects within the state. This ban was implemented to address local concerns and opposition from various stakeholders.

short_description: West Virginia passed Senate Bill 583 in 2020, which restricts utility-scale solar generation capacity.
long_description: Senate Bill 583 of 2020 (S.B. 583) limits utility-scale solar generation capacity by prohibiting any single facility from having a generating capacity greater than 200 MW and setting a cumulative limit of 400 MW for all facilities operating at any given time. It also imposes conditions on the expansion of solar facilities based on energy output sold to residential, commercial, or industrial customers.

short_description: The Beech Ridge Wind Farm faced local opposition and legal challenges, including a lawsuit by the Animal Welfare Institute and Mountain Communities for Responsible Energy.
long_description: The Beech Ridge Wind Farm, a 100-MW wind project in Greenbrier County, was met with local opposition when proposed in 2005. Opponents included the Animal Welfare Institute and Mountain Communities for Responsible Energy. The project faced legal challenges before the Public Service Commission (PSC) and federal court. During the lawsuit, construction proceeded on only 40 out of 124 turbines until a decision was made. In 2009, a federal district court imposed severe restrictions on the project.

short_description: The Mount Storm Wind Project faced legal challenges from landowners in Grant County, leading to a Supreme Court reversal and eventual completion of the project.
long_description: In 2005, landowners in Grant County filed a nuisance lawsuit against Shell WindEnergy, Inc. and NedPower for their planned wind power project. The trial court dismissed the action, but the West Virginia Supreme Court reversed on appeal in June 2007, remanding the case back to the lower court. Despite legal challenges, the 264-MW Mount Storm Wind Project was completed in 2008.

short_description: The Tyr Energy Solar Project faced local opposition over impacts to farmland, wildlife, and rural character.
long_description: Local opposition has arisen regarding the 100-MW Tyr Energy Solar Project in Mason County. Opposition focused on impacts to farmland, wildlife, and the local rural character of the county. Some residents put up signs reading “Stop Solar Farms.” The project was approved by the West Virginia Public Service Commission in December 2023.

short_description: Manitowoc County adopted a wind ordinance in 2013 that required developers to offer annual payments to non-participating landowners and set strict noise limits.
long_description: In 2013, the Manitowoc County Board passed a wind ordinance that was as strict as they could possibly make it while complying with state law. The ordinance requires developers to offer annual payments to all nonparticipating landowners within 0.5 miles of a project, starting at $600 per year for one turbine and limits noise to 35 dBA.

short_description: Cassel adopted a wind energy ordinance in 2023 that limits noise to 35 dBA and requires large turbines to be set back the greater of 1 mile or 10 times turbine height.
long_description: The Town of Cassel, Marathon County, adopted a wind energy ordinance in May 2023 that limits noise to 35 dBA at non-participating property lines and residences and requires large wind turbines to be set back the greater of 1 mile or 10 times turbine height from facility property lines.

long_description: The Town of Cleveland, Marathon County, adopted a wind energy ordinance in June 2023 that limits noise to 35 dBA at non-participating property lines and residences and requires large wind turbines to be set back the greater of 1 mile or 10 times turbine height from facility property lines.

short_description: Courtland adopted a solar energy system licensing ordinance in 2023 that requires setbacks and noise limits.
long_description: The Town of Courtland, Columbia County, adopted a Solar Energy System Licensing Ordinance in July 2023 that requires solar inverters and any sound-producing equipment to be at least 500 feet from non-participating property lines and requires noise at property lines to be limited to 35 dB.

short_description: Lincoln passed a 6-month moratorium on wind energy development in response to RWE Renewables America’s interest in building a wind farm.
long_description: In May 2021, the town of Lincoln, located in Eau Claire County, passed a 6-month moratorium on wind energy development in direct response to RWE Renewables America's interest in building a wind farm. The moratorium received support from several dozen residents at a township meeting.

long_description: The Town of Lowville, Columbia County, adopted a wind energy ordinance in May 2024 that limits noise to 35 dBA at any property line or residence and requires large wind turbines to be set back the greater of 1 mile or 10 times turbine height from property lines.
